records.finding: Tallet’s edition documents daily hieratic reports in Merer’s logbooks on papyrus. The specific catalogue comparison with the blank Hemaka roll is deferred because it is a separate object. The Abydos U-j bone and ivory tags supply a separately dated archaeological witness to the early sign system. The relationship of Egyptian writing to Uruk proto-cuneiform and the significance of separate painted marks on vessels remain open. Also proposes a distinct local receiver at Serabit el-Khadim. Several alphabetic signs there preserve recognizable Egyptian sign forms given Semitic consonantal values; an adapts link describes the graphic inheritance. The Temple of Hathor sphinx gives a local witness of the two scripts used on one object. The early Egyptian source record describes the sign repertoire, and a handoff from any individual Abydos object or a route from Serabit to Lachish remains unresolved.

claim_reviews.rationale: Museum describes Wailwan Country specimen and food preparation over 30,000 years with usewear and starch evidence for flour. Independent faunal geochronology questions common primary context and does not directly date this specimen; age assignment remains contextual.
Grün §6 gives alternative scenarios involving either older primary deposits or redeposition, not proof this specific object moved. Matching specimen to excavated unit remains necessary.

records.finding: Hiscock and colleagues report a single diagnostic fragment with associated charcoal in CG1 A2 excavation unit 52. The later site synthesis's table includes the same Wk-37976 determination, so it is not a second date for the fragment. The more ancient reported evidence from Madjedbebe is a separate Australian site. Similarity and chronology alone leave routes and continuity unresolved. The baseline record is retained.

sources.locator: pp. 3–8, excavation unit 52 and specimen association
sources.note: Original report; one fragment with contextual dating.
Reuses the same charcoal sample from CG1 rather than independently dating a second associated context.

sources.locator: Results, table 2 and Discussion, archaeological comparisons
sources.note: Independent assemblage and age model, not evidence of inter-site transfer.

records.next: Seek securely associated comparative sites and source or mobility evidence capable of distinguishing regional transmission from another local occurrence.
records.name: Carpenter’s Gap ground-edge axe production

review.rationale: No changes proposed; Hiscock original documents a ground-bevel flake with same-unit charcoal 48,875–43,941 cal BP. The attribution and contextual age remain interpretations, and comparative similarity alone does not establish a route or transfer.

claim_reviews.rationale: No new link or record admitted. Separate site evidence cannot establish continuity; original charcoal result is not an independent second date when cited again.

new_discoveries.name: Proto-Sinaitic alphabetic writing at Serabit el-Khadim

date.label: c. 1850–1800 BCE (estimated local use)
date.basis: Parker’s approximate range for local Proto-Sinaitic use rests on dated Egyptian associations and stylistic assessment. The British Museum dates the sphinx to about 1800 BCE.

events.statement: The sandstone sphinx Sinai 345 (British Museum EA41748) has a hieroglyphic inscription naming Hathor and inscriptions in an early Semitic alphabet. Scholars read a dedication to Baʿalat, ‘the Lady’, in the alphabetic text.
events.place_note: Hathor temple at Serabit el-Khadim in southern Sinai
events.caveats: The readings of some signs and the precise chronology remain disputed. The find documents local use of the script.

evidence.supports: Identifies sandstone sphinx, findspot, the two scripts and approximate date.
Analyzes both scripts on Sinai 345 and preserves the stable reading of the dedication while proposing a new reading of the surrounding text.
Uses Egyptian comparanda and archaeological context to assess the date of the sphinx and related local inscriptions.

claim_reviews.path: identity, description, kind, domain, grain, concept, origin, places, known_from
claim_reviews.rationale: Wilson-Wright p. 136 identifies sandstone sphinx, paired scripts, Semitic dedication and temple; Parker p. 269 identifies local consonantal writing. Origin unknown is appropriate.

Parker estimates local use c. 1850–1800 BCE, with typological placement of sphinx in Senwosret III reign; inscriptions are not directly dated, and broader scholarly disagreement is caveated. Wilson-Wright p. 136 reports both scripts, Hathor and the stable Baʿalat reading.
Identifies a named witness rather than the alphabet’s invention and leaves the origin and contact routes open.

Goldwasser pp. 130–132 and Table 13 compares Egyptian eye with Sinai signs; Höflmayer et al. p. 713 recognize eye D4 as source of ʿayin in independently excavated Lachish inscription, while citing overlapping prior comparative scholarship. The directed adaptation is graphic repertoire, not an identified transfer from an individual Abydos object or a specific carrier. Both endpoints inspected.

review.duplicate_screen: Search for Serabit, Proto-Sinaitic and early alphabet in discoveries returned only this proposed record. It is distinct from the Egyptian script source and localized to Serabit.

date.label: 3.040–2.581 million years ago
date.basis: Finestone et al. give these bounds for the NY-1 archaeological context. Plummer et al. give 3.032 Ma for the older limit in their final summary. The interval dates the deposit, with no direct date of collection.

events.statement: Geochemistry and geological field samples support the import of nonlocal stone preserved in the Nyayanga Oldowan assemblage.
events.scope: Local and nonlocal raw material samples compared with artifacts from bed NY-1.

evidence.locator: Results, Sources accessed by hominins and Stone transport distance, Figures 4–5
evidence.supports: No suitable quartzite cobbles occur in the sampled local deposits, and artifact quartzite most closely matches a sampled deposit around 13 km away.

evidence.locator: Results, Stone transport behavior and Figure 6; Discussion
evidence.supports: Outer-surface retention and early-stage pieces support the transport of relatively little-worked stone.
Dates the geological context that contains the specimens assessed for raw material provenance.

review.rationale: Distinct documented procurement practice at the Nyayanga locality; not a duplicate of the flaking event.

claim_reviews.rationale: Finestone compares geological source surveys and artifact chemistry; its Awach drainage sample is around 13 km away. Exact past pickup sites are unresolved, and description says likely.
sources: finestone-2025-nyayanga-stone-transport: Results, Sources accessed and Stone transport distance

claim_reviews.rationale: The archaeological assemblage is assigned to bed NY-1 dated 3.040–2.581 Ma by Finestone; Plummer gives a different older bound, recorded explicitly. Results include excavated and surface artifacts targeted to upper NY-1, and transport inference from comparisons and reduction indicators; neither exact journey nor direct date of collection is claimed.
sources: finestone-2025-nyayanga-stone-transport: Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion

review.duplicate_screen: Procurement practice is a distinct bounded activity from existing NY-1 flaking and tissue-processing event; no separate record for the same procurement identified.

new_discoveries.name: Split oak timbers for Linear Pottery wells

date.label: 5256–5255 BCE (felling of trees for the horizontal planks)
date.basis: Tree-ring dates for the trees used for the main horizontal planks; splitting and installation followed.

events.statement: Woodworkers at Ostrov made the horizontal oak planks for the well lining mainly by radial splitting. The analysed lining also contains one tangentially split plank.

evidence.locator: §3.1 Trace evidence, table 1, figs. 6–8; §3.2 Dendrochronology and radiocarbon dating
evidence.supports: The Ostrov study reports a separately excavated application, mainly radially split oak planks with one tangentially split plank.
Tree-ring dating identifies the felling years of trees used for the original horizontal planks. Repairs and posts have separate dates.

date.label: 5102 BCE timber felling to 5099 BCE construction-pit plank
date.basis: The lining timbers derive from oaks felled in 5102 BCE. The authors use a separate pit plank dated to 5099 BCE to infer the start of well construction.

events.statement: The Altscherbitz well lining used oak beams split radially and tangentially.

evidence.locator: Results, Well A, figs. 3–4, S8 and S9
evidence.supports: The researchers reconstructed splitting from the timbers and tree-ring series. They identify oak beams split radially and tangentially from the trees used in Well A.

claim_reviews.path: identity, description, kind, domain, origin and places
claim_reviews.rationale: Tegel Results Well A and Vostrovská §§3.1–3.2 document split oak at separate central European LBK wells; origin unknown avoids invention or contact claims.

Vostrovská §3.1 table 1, figs. 6–8 and §3.2 documents radial and one tangential plank, felling years 5256–5255 BC, with posts and repairs separately dated. Felling is not exact time of every processing step.
Tegel Results Well A identifies radial and tangential splitting, 5102 BCE felling and a 5099 BCE pit plank; latter is construction-onset inference.
Ostrov is earlier among the two cases, with dates explicitly felling or associated material, and origin and transfer left unknown.

review.duplicate_screen: Distinct regional material preparation practice versus existing Altscherbitz wedged joinery frame; both local and earlier separate Ostrov event retained without asserting transmission.

new_discoveries.name: Mixed meat and dairy cattle husbandry at Ludwinowo 7

date.label: Ludwinowo 7 phases IIB and III, c. 5230–5025 cal BCE
date.basis: Outer bounds of the two modelled phase ranges cited by Smyth et al. §2.2 at 68% probability. These are context ages.

events.statement: Age-at-death profiles and tooth isotopes at Ludwinowo support a mixed cattle economy with seasonal calving and increased retention of older animals in phase III.
events.caveats: The authors infer herd management from age distributions and isotopes. The sampled tooth ages do not identify each animal’s sex or its individual use.

evidence.supports: Numbers of identified remains and age data show cattle predominance in the domestic herd; the authors infer meat and secondary-product use.
Phase-specific mortality and enamel isotope profiles support a mixed meat and dairy herd. The cattle studied calved over an estimated four to five months.

review.rationale: A distinct local husbandry practice from sieve processing; no duplicate discovered.

claim_reviews.rationale: Osypińska 2019 §7.1.4 and Smyth 2023 §§3.3–3.5 and 4 support predominantly cattle, interpreted mixed meat and milk economy, seasonal calving and phase III older-animal retention.
Smyth 2023 §§2.2–2.4 and 3.3–3.5 dates the site and phases and identifies isotopic and mortality evidence. 68% phase bounds and unknown individual sex and use are acknowledged.

date.label: About 23,000 calibrated years BP
date.basis: Approximate occupational context of the Ohalo II blades. Calibrated BP uses 1950 as its reference.

events.statement: At Ohalo II, wear on two flint blades is consistent with the use of hafted tools to cut near-ripe cereal stems.
events.scope: Hafted cereal cutting at Ohalo II
events.caveats: The hafts are inferred from wear. Their form and number of inserts remain unknown, as do the scale of use and which recovered grains came from this method.

evidence.supports: Cutting wear on five flint blades resembles experimental wear from cutting near-ripe cereal stems. Two blades, AL73c and AJ39c, carry wear interpreted as evidence of hafting.

claim_reviews.rationale: 2016 original results and figures 5–6 report two blades with inferred haft wear and near-ripe cereal wear. Site context around 23,000 cal BP; caveats appropriately qualify inference, insert count and connection to other grains. Name, description, practice/food foraging, site place, event, date, earliest record, basis, caveats and note supported within stated bounds.

review.duplicate_screen: Different objects and functional practice from Ohalo grinding record; open lead concerns stronger multi-insert claim.

new_discoveries.name: Early Natufian plant grinding and pounding at Shubayqa 1

date.label: Approximately 14,800–14,100 cal BP (12,850–12,150 BCE)
date.basis: Pedersen and colleagues give this Early Natufian contextual estimate for phases 4–7 at 68.2% using IntCal20, with 1950 as the BP reference.

events.statement: Ground stone tools from Early Natufian Shubayqa 1 bear wear consistent with grinding seeds or cereals, and with grinding or pounding tubers or similar soft plant material.
events.scope: Ground stone tool use in Early Natufian occupation phases at Shubayqa 1
events.caveats: The Early Natufian sample is small. Wear suggests classes of plant material. Individual plant identifications, the precise use of each tool, and any tool-to-food-fragment assignment remain uncertain.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, Early Natufian Use-Wear, table 2 and fig. 4
evidence.supports: In Early Natufian Shubayqa 1, wear on a handstone suggests seed or cereal grinding. Wear on a combined quern and mortar and nearby tool is consistent with grinding or pounding tubers or similar soft plants. The excavators compare these traces with food remains of the same broad period.

evidence.locator: Section 3.1, Shubayqa Sites, Setting and Dating
evidence.supports: Radiocarbon context for Early Natufian phases 4–7 is approximately 14,800–14,100 cal BP.

claim_reviews.rationale: 2026 analysis reports Early Natufian phase 4–7 context 14800–14100 cal BP at 68.2% IntCal20; small tool sample gives seed/cereal and tuber-like use-wear interpretations. Identity, practice, food processing, Jordan, event, dates, earliest record, basis and caveats fit observed contextual and interpretive limits.

review.duplicate_screen: Ground stone artifacts constitute a distinct practice from charred food remains; same local occupation, not inferred continuity.

new_discoveries.name: Inferred firewood gathering at Gesher Benot Ya‘aqov

date.label: Approximately 0.78–0.79 million years ago
date.basis: The charcoal horizon is Layer II-6 Level 1 (MIS 18). The displayed range is the site's approximate age used in the Gesher fire record.

events.statement: In Layer II-6 Level 1, charcoal and unburnt wood include abundant ash and olive. Comparison of taxa and their distributions led the analysts to infer collection of locally available firewood.

evidence.supports: The charcoal taxa and spatial concentrations in Level 1 inform the authors' interpretation of local fuel procurement.

evidence.locator: Spatial Analysis and Fire at Gesher Benot Ya‘aqov
evidence.supports: Reported approximate age of the site.

claim_reviews.rationale: Allué attributes local wood gathering for fire to inferred human behavior based on charcoal and wood from one horizon; deadwood/driftwood is a suggested source. Site and lake Hula context are explicit.

Level 1 taxa and ash/olive abundance are documented, while collecting and use are inference; 0.78–0.79 Ma is the existing approximate site-age convention rather than a dated duration or precise interval.

review.duplicate_screen: The fire record describes repeated combustion, while this node addresses inferred fuel gathering in Level 1. Related interpretations are not asserted as two independent observations.

date.label: Site context approximately 7964–6299 cal BP
date.basis: Rosenberg and colleagues, Table 1, date KS 2 by the site. The outer bounds combine different dated site samples, with cal BP converted to BCE using the 1950 reference.

events.statement: Waterlogged basket fragments catalogued as KS 2 preserve alternate pair-twining and were deposited in a pit with olive stones.

evidence.supports: The surviving form and weave are described directly. The assigned age derives from the site context.

claim_reviews.path: /identity, description, kind, domain, grain, concept, places
claim_reviews.rationale: Rosenberg identifies three KS2 twig basket fragments, alternate pair-twining, and a clay-filled olive-bearing pit in central Kfar Samir. Function is not established.

Table 1 dates KS2 by the general site chronology and gives two outer sample intervals 7964–7431 and 6531–6299 cal BP; the broad displayed envelope converts these to 6014–4349 BCE. This is not a direct basket date and may include unoccupied intervals.

review.duplicate_screen: No existing exact Kfar Samir basketry record; distinct craft object from inferred oil extraction. Similar woven basketry elsewhere does not imply transmission.

new_discoveries.name: Ruminant dairy use in pottery at Tell Sabi Abyad

date.label: ca. 6400–6330 cal BCE, Operation IV
date.basis: Context of SAB263 as given in Table 2.

events.statement: A Grey Burnished Ware body sherd from Operation IV yielded a ruminant dairy lipid signature.

evidence.supports: The excavated sherd has the earliest contextual date among the dairy positives.

date.label: ca. 6000–5900 cal BCE, Transitional period
date.basis: Dates for the three later dairy positives in Table 2.

events.statement: Two Dark-Faced Burnished Ware and one Standard Fine Ware sherd from the Transitional period yielded ruminant dairy lipid signatures.

evidence.locator: Table 2, samples SAB2, SAB173 and SAB214; §4.4
evidence.supports: The later sherds provide multiple dairy positives in a distinct occupation phase.

claim_reviews.path: identity, description, classification, origin, places, earliest_record, events and caveats
claim_reviews.rationale: Original lipid study Table 2 and §4.4 reports SAB263 GBW 6400–6330 and SAB2, SAB173, SAB214 in 6000–5900 contexts as ruminant dairy; sample identifies vessel contact, not species or processing method. Classification is bounded site practice.

claim_reviews.relation: companion_of: pottery and dairy use worked together in the local arrangement evidenced by SAB263. Direction points from local dairy contact to regional pottery capability; does not imply dependence on the earliest dated event or transmission.
claim_reviews.independent_corroboration: 2010 excavation provides separate evidence of local pottery; 2015 isotopes directly identify contact in a later sherd. Same site investigators overlap, and these are not independent replicate assays. For this narrow material use, the sherd itself is direct evidence, corroborated by independently excavated early pottery assemblage; no causal transmission is asserted.
claim_reviews.rationale: The 2015 study Table 2 and §4.4 report a ruminant-dairy signature in this actual Grey Burnished Ware sherd. The local vessel and the dairy product form one observed arrangement. Manufacturing provenance and how this relates to the first regional pottery are unknown. companion_of matches vocab.json; uses_instrument was an error because it is limited to instruments of observation.

review.duplicate_screen: Distinct local dairy contact with pottery; no Sabi Abyad dairy record in current snapshot; dates and community differ from other dairy nodes.

new_discoveries.name: Possible potting turntable at Tell Feres al-Sharqi

date.label: ca. 4700 BCE, Late Ubaid workshop
date.basis: The original comparative study places the workshop discovery in the local Late Ubaid phase at about 4700 BCE.

events.statement: A clay disc about 26 cm in diameter with a shallow possible pivot socket was recovered in the pottery workshop.

evidence.supports: Describes and dates the disc and discusses possible rotary use.
Documents potting equipment with the excavated workshop, including possible turntable disc fragments.

events.caveats: Its interpretation as a turntable is provisional. This is workshop context dating.

claim_reviews.rationale: Baldi and Roux original comparison §Tell Feres gives ca. 4700 BCE workshop clay disc about 26 cm with possible pivot socket; later rotary forming marks around 3900 BCE. Dating is context not invention; function and continuity properly tentative. 2014 is same excavation lineage, not independent corroboration.

review.duplicate_screen: Separate dated workshop object from later wheel-coiling capability; no matching object record found.

date.label: Approximately 7700–7550 cal BP (5750–5600 BCE)
date.basis: Zong and colleagues’ interpretation of the studied Kuahuqiao sequence. Calibrated BP uses 1950 as its reference year.

events.statement: Sediment and plant remains indicate rice cultivation in a coastal wetland at Kuahuqiao.
events.scope: Cultivation inferred for the Kuahuqiao occupation sequence studied by Zong and colleagues.
events.caveats: The date describes the studied sequence. The evidence gives no excavated field layout or exact cultivation start date.

evidence.supports: Sediment and biological indicators support rice cultivation in a managed wetland in the sampled occupation interval.
Independent morphology of excavated rice grains and husks supports early cultivation at Kuahuqiao.

review.rationale: New local wetland cultivation evidence is a distinct site and context from later Lake Tai engineered fields and from Shangshan rice morphology.

claim_reviews.rationale: Zong describes a Kuahuqiao coastal wetland and associated rice and wild-food remains; Zheng examines rice morphology. Burning taxa are disputed by Shu and barrier construction remains a proposal.

Zong dates cultural sediments in this specific sequence about 7700–7550 cal BP and interprets combined sediment indicators and rice remains as cultivation; Zheng supports cultivation using different rice specimens. Converted dates are correct and approximate.
Only the sampled sequence is dated. The contrasted oak/pine interpretation and unverified barrier are disclosed as unresolved.

unknowns: The inferred wetland does not itself document an excavated field layout or transfer to later systems.

date.label: 4493–4365 cal BCE, associated Feature 3 sample
date.basis: Published 2σ bounds for MAMS22081, the associated radiocarbon sample from Feature 3 in Trench 24.

events.statement: A worked copper ring or band, C_P2/13, was present in Trench 24 at Pločnik. Its microstructure contains slip lines and annealing twins.
events.scope: Copper artefact C_P2/13, Trench 24, spit 9, Horizon 1, Feature 3.
events.caveats: The date applies to the associated feature. The study finds wider evidence for secondary processing at the settlement. The place and time of making this individual object remain unresolved.

evidence.supports: The find is ordinary copper with traces of working and annealing, dated by context.

review.rationale: A specific copper ring C_P2/13 is distinct from Pločnik tin-bronze foil 63 and is a new bounded object-level witness.

claim_reviews.rationale: 2021 Pločnik report identifies copper ring in Vinča occupation and metallography; isotope study groups it with Belovode residues, without establishing exchange.
C_P2/13 is T24/F3, S9, horizon 1; associated MAMS22081 is 4493–4365 cal BCE, and Fig.12 documents slip lines and annealing twins. Sample dates context rather than individual manufacture.

Question asks whether Belovode smelting supplied copper for this specific ring; Group 3 groups C_P2/13 with B47/12/3 and B23/12 but cannot discriminate shared geological source from movement of metal.
claim_reviews.direction: Belovode feature to Pločnik band hypothesized only
claim_reviews.context: Dispersed isotope group; direction and physical route unresolved
claim_reviews.independent_corroboration: No independent replication of specific supply, chapters share project samples and authors

claim_reviews.rationale: Source basis is appropriate and missing discriminants are stated.

new_discoveries.name: Spun cotton yarn at Huaca Prieta

date.label: 6882–6657 cal BP (c. 4930–4710 BCE)
date.basis: Dillehay et al. Table 1 reports the site’s 2σ calibrated range for cotton yarn AA82121.

events.statement: A cotton yarn dated to 6882–6657 cal BP was recovered from the upper part of stratum 52 in Huaca Prieta’s HP-3 trench.
events.caveats: This date applies to the yarn sample. Its place of manufacture and the spinning equipment are unknown.

evidence.supports: Directly dates the early cotton yarn.
Describes AA82121 as an earlier cotton yarn without the indigo decoration of the younger striped textiles.
Separate structural catalogue describes variation in loose yarns and yarns in fabrics from the Huaca Prieta assemblage.

review.rationale: Dillehay 2012 Table 1 directly dates a cotton yarn in stratum 52 to 6882–6657 cal BP; Splitstoser 2016 confirms the same assay. The sample is distinct from the indigo-bearing textile, and production site is unknown. Splitstoser 2017 Table 12.5 identifies single and complex yarns and interprets their varied dimensions in relation to fabric types.

claim_reviews.paths: id; name; summary; kind; domain; grain; origin; places; known_from; events/0; earliest_record; research

claim_reviews.rationale: Splitstoser chapter p. 475–476 and Table 12.5 report loose and fabric yarn structures and interpret dimensions as suited to different fabrics.

new_discoveries.name: Mounded planting plots at Kuk Swamp

date.label: 6950–6440 cal BP (c. 5000–4490 BCE)
date.basis: Calibrated radiocarbon chronology of the early Phase 2 palaeosurface, including charcoal sampled from basal fills; 1950 BP reference.

events.statement: Excavated early Phase 2 surfaces at Kuk Swamp preserve bases of regularly spaced earthen mounds and the cut features between them. The excavators interpret these as traces of cultivation on raised plots.

evidence.supports: Describes excavated mound bases, interprets their function in cultivation, and reports a separate plant proxy favouring deliberate banana planting in Phase 2.
Excavated Phase 2 surfaces date to 6950–6440 cal BP. The authors interpret the concentrations in early feature fills as evidence of bananas deliberately planted in mounded plots.

events.caveats: Only the bases and adjacent fills survive. The source range dates the relevant palaeosurface rather than the construction of individual mounds.

review.rationale: Distinct local land-preparation practice from the crop-specific banana record; no pre-existing mounded-process record found in base. The candidate points from banana use to this practice, with no external transmission claim.

claim_reviews.rationale: Early Phase 2 palaeosurface shows bases of former mounds and intervening cut features interpreted as cultivation on raised plots along the wetland; interpretation and physical evidence are distinguished.
Basal-fill charcoal supports 6950–6440 cal BP for the early palaeosurface; preserved bases and adjacent cuts imply raised plots. Age is contextual, not direct dating of individual mound construction.
Scoped to earliest documented Kuk mound palaeosurface, with no world priority or origin claim; basis is sourced and status draft.

date.label: c. 164,000 years ago
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: The excavation's leader states that at 164,000 years ago (about 162,050 BCE) people in coastal South Africa expanded their diet to include shellfish and other marine resources.

evidence.supports: Our findings show that at 164,000 years ago in coastal South Africa humans expanded their diet to include shellfish and other marine resources, perhaps as a response to harsh environmental conditions

date.label: Approximately 8400 cal BCE
date.basis: Stiner et al. infer initial small-scale caprine management at about 8400 cal BCE within the early sequence.

event.statement: The expanded excavation analysis infers that residents raised small numbers of captured wild caprines in their settlement around 8400 cal BCE.
event.caveats: The earliest phase is inferred from contexts and faunal remains. Urine salts combine human and animal inputs. Capture and rearing preceded substantial captive breeding.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Results and Discussion, The Domesticatory Process at Aşıklı Höyük
evidence.supports: Faunal profiles and evidence of confinement support early small-scale management near 8400 cal BCE, followed by increasingly substantial reproduction in captivity.
Sediment measurements indicate increasing urine-salt deposition from humans and animals during the occupation, contributing a separate proxy for the scale of confinement.

date.label: 4724–4555 cal BCE, associated Feature 6 sample
date.basis: Published 2σ radiocarbon range for the animal-bone sample MAMS23380 associated with Feature 6 in Trench 18.

event.statement: Slag and a slagged sherd were excavated around Feature 6 at Belovode. The analyses support the use of manganese-rich copper ore. The cluster of debris and a burnt, bowl-shaped feature suggest a pottery-lined smelting pit.
event.caveats: The sample dates the associated feature. The lining and precise use of Feature 6 remain archaeological inferences.

evidence.supports: Distinct debris and an associated radiocarbon date in the 2012–2013 excavation.

evidence.locator: pp. 133–138 and 149–151, sherd analysis and conclusion
evidence.supports: Nearby slagged ceramics support the pit-lining interpretation and analyses corroborate the ore characteristics.

date.label: Early Natufian, approximately 13,000–11,600 cal BCE
date.basis: Haklay and Gopher assign Shelter 1 to Early Natufian Layer II. The approximate phase bounds are the regional chronology given by Bocquentin and Noûs.

event.statement: Haklay and Gopher describe a lime-plastered bench in Shelter 1 at Eynan (Ain Mallaha), which they assign to Early Natufian Layer II.
event.caveats: The date is a regional phase range applied to the architectural context. The feature’s function remains debated.

evidence.locator: The Early Natufian architectural remains, fig. 1
evidence.supports: The architectural study describes a plastered bench in Early Natufian Shelter 1 (Layer II) and discusses its debated function.
The authors give a regional Early Natufian date of about 13,000–11,600 cal BCE.

date.label: Approximately 55,000–47,000 years ago
date.basis: Clarkson et al. report Levallois dominance across the sampled strata over about 55–47 ka. Their date for stratum E is 47.5 ± 2.0 ka. Plot coordinates approximate the stated interval.

event.statement: Levallois artifacts remained prominent in later deposits at Dhaba 2 and Dhaba 3.
event.scope: Dhaba 3 strata K and J and Dhaba 2 strata I through E, within the same site locality as the earlier Dhaba 1 evidence.
event.caveats: Clarkson and colleagues did not identify this technique above stratum E. The excavated sequence alone cannot date regional abandonment or demonstrate continuous occupation.

evidence.locator: Results, lithic assemblage; Figures 3–5 and Table 1
evidence.supports: The paper reports dominance in the younger Dhaba 2 and 3 assemblages, absence above stratum E, and luminescence ages on the deposits.

date.label: Attested at Paredones, 6775–6504 cal BP
date.basis: The calibrated range dates a husk and shank attached to cob Par_N1. It bounds the recipient evidence rather than dating a journey.

event.statement: Cultivated maize of Mesoamerican ancestry is attested on the Peruvian coast by the dated Paredones specimen Par_N1. Broader genetic comparisons independently support human dispersal of the crop from Mexico into South America.
event.scope: Regional movement of the crop to the Peruvian coast, as dated by the Paredones attestation.
event.caveats: The donor population, movement route and time of arrival are unresolved. Studies differ over when domestication traits became fixed in the South American lineages.

evidence.locator: Table 1, Paleogenomic characterization, Fig. 3 and Discussion
evidence.supports: Directly dates the attached husk and shank and includes genetic analysis of the same Par_N1 specimen.
Independent genomes support the Mesoamerican ancestry and southward movement of the ancestral crop.

date.label: Approximately 8600–8200 cal BCE (Well 116 fill samples)
date.basis: The excavator’s synthesis of three short-lived cereal samples from fills 123 and 124, table 11.1; this dates material from the fill.

event.statement: Three charred cereal samples from two fills of Well 116 at Kissonerga-Mylouthkia date to roughly 8600–8200 cal BCE in the excavator’s synthesis.

evidence.supports: The final report records sample provenance and age estimates. Well 116 existed before those fills accumulated.

date.label: 8240–7820 BCE (associated seed, 95.4%)
date.basis: AMS measurement BA07888 on a cork-tree seed from a deposit containing charred foxtail millet.

event.statement: Flotation at Donghulin recovered charred grains that excavators identified morphologically as foxtail millet. A seed from one millet-bearing deposit dates its context to 8240–7820 BCE.
event.scope: One dated millet-bearing deposit from a four-deposit assemblage.
event.caveats: The available radiocarbon date is on associated material. Tiny grains can move between layers, and morphology is the basis for the domesticated-type identification.

evidence.supports: Identifies charred foxtail millet in four deposits and dates an associated cork-tree seed from one deposit.

date.label: Middle of the 34th century BCE, Naqada IIIA2 (approximate)
date.basis: The ceramics assign the tomb to Naqada IIIA2. Görsdorf and colleagues’ relative and radiocarbon chronology places this phase near the middle of the 34th century BCE. The displayed interval indexes the century of their estimate. The wood samples date material from the tomb rather than the inscribed tags.

event.statement: Excavators recovered small drilled bone and ivory tags with incised signs in Tomb U-j at Abydos. Dreyer reads some signs as early phonetic writing and interprets the tags as labels attached to goods.
event.place_note: Tomb U-j, Cemetery U at Umm el-Qaab, Abydos
event.caveats: The tags attest to early writing in a funerary context. Individual readings and the original uses of the tags are debated.

evidence.supports: Findspot, phase attribution, materials and drilled tags. The readings of phonetic signs and the use as labels are the excavator’s interpretations.

evidence.locator: p. 641, Table 1 on pp. 642–644, conclusion on p. 644
evidence.supports: The tomb was dated archaeologically to Naqada IIIA2. The phase estimate is based on dated material including wood from the tomb.

date.label: Late in Khufu’s reign (placed c. 2550–2520 BCE by Tallet)
date.basis: The dated Wadi el-Jarf archive places the logs late in Khufu’s reign. The numerical range is Tallet’s approximate chronology of the reign as a whole.

event.statement: Scribes entered daily work reports in hieratic, a cursive form of the Egyptian hieroglyphic system, on the papyrus sheets of Merer’s logbooks.
event.place_note: Wadi el-Jarf is the findspot. The logs document work at several locations.
event.scope: Papyrus Jarf A and B, the logbooks concerning Inspector Merer’s team.

evidence.locator: PDF pp. 2, 5–8, 16 (cover summary and Annex I)
evidence.supports: The edition identifies the A and B fragments as two hieratic logbooks from late in Khufu’s reign. The translation preserves daily entries about Inspector Merer’s team.

evidence.locator: Sources and Contexts of Inked Hieratic, subsection on the 2nd to 6th Dynasties, Fig. 1
evidence.supports: Documents the handwriting and physical support of Papyrus Jarf BIV from the reign of Khufu and describes preserved entries within the ruled format.
Provides the approximate calendar range for Khufu’s reign.

date.label: ca. 9000–7500 cal BP, sampled Jiahu contexts
date.basis: Occupational range used by Liu and colleagues. The year bounds use 1950 as the BP reference.

event.statement: Rice starch, damaged starch, and fungal remains consistent with Monascus were found in Jiahu vessels. The investigators interpret the combination as evidence for mould-starter brewing, with some possible malt processing.

evidence.supports: Reports the context range, plant and fungal remains, and attribution of likely functions for globular jars and bottles.

event.caveats: The damaged starch and fungal morphologies are interpreted together. The same fragments have not been matched across the chemical and microfossil studies.

date.label: Ludwinowo 7 phases IIB and III, c. 5230–5025 cal BCE
date.basis: Outer bounds of the two modelled phase ranges cited by Smyth et al. §2.2 at 68% probability. These are context ages.

event.statement: Ruminant dairy fats occur in perforated ceramic vessels from phases IIB and III at Ludwinowo 7.
event.caveats: The vessel forms and residues support dairy straining. The species and recipe cannot be identified from sieve fats alone.

evidence.supports: Reports ruminant dairy fats in perforated fragments from LBK phases IIB and III at Ludwinowo.

date.label: c. 2500–2450 BCE, Khufu and Khafra assemblage
date.basis: The analysts' approximate chronological range for the two reigns represented by sealings in the Giza debris.

event.statement: The Dynasty 4 settlement debris at Giza contains a full-size arsenical-copper chisel and fragments identified as probable axe blades of the same material. The excavation and analysis supply evidence for working tools alongside the better-known funerary kits.
event.scope: Finished artisan tools from the Giza Kromer debris dump.
event.caveats: The material was redeposited. Dating and the association with carpentry apply to the assemblage. Individual tools cannot be assigned to a particular reign or workpiece.

evidence.supports: Royal sealings associate the redeposited assemblage with the reigns of Khufu and Khafra. Analysis identified arsenical copper in a full-size chisel and two probable axe-blade fragments.

date.label: 10,494–10,146 cal BCE, unit 2 layer 5 shell
date.basis: Published calibrated bounds for shell sample Beta-280992 in unit 2 layer 5, with the article's local marine-reservoir correction.

event.statement: The central trench contains an early iron-oxide extraction deposit with rocks from the vein and stone mining tools.
event.caveats: The shell supplies a contextual date dependent on reservoir correction. The age of the first extraction and the dates of particular tools remain unresolved.

evidence.locator: pp. 466–470, Figs. 3 and 6 and Table 1, Beta-280992
evidence.supports: The dated early shell comes from unit 2 layer 5. Figures 3 and 6 show the extraction and deposit contexts, and the authors associate the date with early central-trench mining.

date.label: 2398–1954 cal BCE, unit 2 layer 3 charcoal
date.basis: Published calibrated bounds for charcoal sample UGAMS 5443 in unit 2 layer 3.

event.statement: Late Archaic miners returned to the trench after sediment had accumulated over early workings. Unit 2 preserves Late Archaic deposits above the earlier mining levels.
event.caveats: The charcoal dates an associated mining deposit. The date applies to this excavated layer within a separately documented phase of extraction.

evidence.locator: pp. 466–470, Figs. 3 and 6 and Table 1, UGAMS 5443
evidence.supports: Late and early archaeological levels in the central trench are separated by a natural colluvial deposit. Charcoal from the later level dates to 2398–1954 cal BCE.

date.label: Dongodien context, c. 5000–4500 cal BP
date.basis: Grillo et al. Table 1 gives the site range. The calendar years use the dataset’s 1950 BP conversion.

event.statement: One residue from a ceramic vessel at the Dongodien herder-fisher settlement falls in the ruminant dairy range.
event.place_note: Dongodien (GaJi4) on the eastern shore of Lake Turkana.
event.caveats: This is one of five interpretable residues at the site. The range applies to the site context. Herd species, degree of dietary reliance, and exact dairy preparation remain unresolved.

evidence.locator: Table 1; Lipid residue results, Meat and milk; Fig. 4
evidence.supports: Dongodien yielded a pottery residue in the ruminant dairy range, alongside evidence for other animal and possible plant products.

date.label: 1.79–1.07 million years ago
date.basis: Table 1 brackets the deposit between the Olduvai and Jaramillo subchrons. The fossils were not individually dated. Integer plot coordinates use the record's approximate before-1950 convention.

event.statement: Marin-Monfort and colleagues identified burned small mammal bones in Wonderwerk Cave Stratum 11, deep within the cave and associated with Acheulean artifacts.
event.caveats: The investigators interpret the location and distribution as evidence consistent with repeated fire introduction by hominins. The source of ignition, use of a hearth and specific activities remain unresolved.

evidence.supports: Reports the sampled layer and its geological age bracket.
The study finds heating signatures on small mammal bones and reports their spatial distribution in the cave.

date.label: 5,500 to 5,100 cal BP (c. 3550 to 3150 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: In Phase II-2 at Los Morteros, builders erected brick walls on stone and mortar foundations. Excavators place room use at 5,500–5,100 cal BP, using stratigraphy and dated offerings associated with closure.

evidence.locator: The Adobes of Los Morteros, Fig. 1 and Table 1
evidence.supports: Documents the walls and their earlier and closing contexts. Table 1 records no radiocarbon sample directly dating the Phase II-2 architecture.

evidence.locator: Results, Structure and Grain Size of Adobe Bricks, Figs. 2–4
evidence.supports: Lamination, fine sediment and comparison with samples from a modern flood deposit support cutting blocks from naturally laid clay.

event.caveats: The dated offerings and earlier deposits constrain the building chronology. The walls were not directly dated, and the exact clay source remains open.

date.label: 8400–8300 calibrated BCE
date.basis: Approximate date reported by Mäkelä and Kunnas and Bender Jørgensen et al. Other published age estimates or site-level calibrations use different samples or treatments.

event.statement: The surviving Antrea fishing net is made of knotted willow-bast cordage. Its published knot drawing was identified as a form of sheet bend.

evidence.supports: Fishing net remains of willow bast, with other objects, are dated to 8400–8300 calibrated BCE; the suggested boat context is an interpretation.
The authors report a willow-bast fishing net with knots, floats and sinkers dated 8400–8300 cal BC at Antrea in present-day Russia.

evidence.locator: pp. 479–481, Discussion: Cultural transmission, task differentiation, and the deep past of knots; Fig. 1E
evidence.supports: Reanalyses the published Antrea knot and identifies it as the sheet-bend form shown in Figure 1E. The analysis compares other sites and leaves transfer versus convergence open.

event.caveats: This find witnesses mesh fishing. Boat loss is an interpretation. A reanalysis of the published knot drawing identifies the structure; historical transmission to later nets remains open.

date.label: by c. 3100 BCE
date.basis: Approximate date assigned to the macehead scene by Manning (section 4).

event.statement: The Scorpion macehead from Hierakonpolis shows a ruler holding a hoe. The original excavation publication reads the lower part of the carving as work on an irrigation canal, and Manning dates the scene to about 3100 BCE.

evidence.supports: Such artificial irrigation of the fields is attested at the every beginning of unified Egyptian history (The so-called “Scorpion Macehead” depicting the king clearing a canal ca. 3100 BC)

evidence.locator: pp. 9–10, note to Pl. XXVIc and Pl. XXVIc
evidence.supports: The original excavation publication describes the carved scene and reads it as inauguration of canal works.
Discusses both the irrigation reading and Schenkel's dissent and distinguishes the older depiction from evidence of basin systems.

event.caveats: The scene is an interpreted depiction. The irrigation purpose is disputed, and the carving does not establish the layout or extent of artificial basin systems at that date.

date.label: By approximately 50,000 years ago
date.basis: A 2022 review reports scattered younger dating estimates and describes the Katanda points as no younger than approximately 50,000 years; the nominal BCE bound is rounded and is not a first-use date.

event.statement: By approximately 50,000 years ago, people represented at Katanda 9 had shaped, barbed bone points available within their local tool assemblage.
event.scope: Crafted bone points with unilateral barbs represented in the Katanda archaeological assemblage; exact mounting is not established.
event.population: People represented by the Katanda 9 archaeological assemblage
event.caveats: The reported age estimates are scattered: an original figure is about 90,000 years, while a later assessment described the chronology as inconclusive and no younger than approximately 50,000 years. An individually documented fishing episode, a detachable line, and the specific use-wear of this point are not established here. The possible much older Olduvai barbed specimen remains contested.

evidence.supports: Reports multiple crafted unilaterally barbed points and preforms at Katanda, and describes the scattered chronological assessment.
Reviews Katanda barbed bone points and earlier unbarbed points, with a contested possible much older Olduvai point.
Identifies a Katanda barbed bone point and interprets it as related to fish capture.
The original excavation report identifies barbed and unbarbed worked bone in the Katanda Middle Stone Age. Its older age interpretation has been reassessed.

date.label: ca. 3500–2900 BCE, original Period V assignment
date.basis: Context range used by Michel and colleagues for Period V. It is the original report’s broad context chronology.

event.statement: A Feigl test gave a positive oxalate result for pale interior deposits sampled from the crisscross grooves of a double-handled jug in the Period V Oval complex. The original investigators interpreted this as evidence consistent with beer.

evidence.supports: Provides the contextual period range, sherd description, result and comparison controls.

evidence.locator: Direct Evidence for Prehistoric Fermented Beverages
evidence.supports: Independently explains why the method and marker do not securely identify beer.

event.caveats: No direct date or independently specific beer marker is available for the tested deposits.

date.label: By about 191,000 years ago
date.basis: Mazza et al. give a pre-isotope-stage-6 geological and faunal attribution. The approximate 191 ka minimum follows the later table by Niekus et al. and is not a direct artifact date.

event.statement: At Campitello, two stone flakes were partly covered with manufactured birch-bark tar, consistent with use as a backing or adhesive.
event.scope: Birch-bark tar partly covering two unretouched stone flakes.
applications: Backing or possible attachment of stone tools
event.caveats: The original Campitello report supplies the chemical identification and associates the finds with geological and faunal evidence. The precise age, production method, tool function and presence of a handle remain uncertain.

evidence.locator: Late Pleistocene Adhesives and table 1; Procedural Complexity and Hafting Practices
evidence.supports: Reports two Campitello flakes, birch-bark tar identification and biochronostratigraphic minimum age >191 ka; the flakes have no clear organic-handle evidence.
Reports the association of two residue-bearing flakes with a gravel and clay deposit and associated fauna. The archaeological context supplies the age estimate.
Primary chemical analyses detected compounds consistent with birch tar on the Campitello flakes.

date.label: 5440–5310 cal BP (c. 3490–3360 BCE)
date.basis: Zarrillo et al. Table 1 gives the calibrated range for directly dated charred residue PLD-005, Beta-312078.

event.statement: In charred residue from ceramic sherd PLD-005, researchers identified Theobroma starch, theobromine and a DNA signal specific to T. cacao. They radiocarbon dated the bulk charred residue.

evidence.locator: p. 1881, Table 1, PLD-005 and note a, and Fig. 2d
evidence.supports: Gives the calibrated age of the bulk residue and distinguishes DNA capture evidence for T. cacao from starch identifiable as Theobroma.

event.caveats: The range applies to the residue on PLD-005. The cacao-positive stirrup-spout bottles came from later tomb contexts.

date.label: Eastern mound occupation approximately 7400–6200 BCE
date.basis: The stated range or year applies to the described evidence or documentary event; it does not establish invention.

event.statement: The site description reports 18 occupation levels on the eastern mound dated 7400–6200 BCE and clustered roof-access houses.

evidence.supports: The site description reports 18 occupation levels on the eastern mound dated 7400–6200 BCE and clustered roof-access houses.
The excavation reports curved plaster to accommodate a feature such as a ladder and heavily trampled floor near the proposed roof access.
The project director reports the blocked entrance found in Building 3 and interprets it as ground-level access in at least some phases.
The site description reports 18 occupation levels on the eastern mound dated 7400–6200 BCE and clustered roof-access houses.

date.label: Approximately 9800 cal BP (7850 BCE)
date.basis: Approximate archaeological context; calibrated BP values use 1950 as reference.

event.statement: At Chogha Golan, residents had access to emmer wheat with domestication-type traits in an early agricultural setting.

evidence.supports: The abstract reports domesticated-type emmer around 9800 cal BP in a long local archaeobotanical sequence.

evidence.locator: Chogha Golan, Sampling and laboratory methods, and Conclusion
evidence.supports: Study of the local sequence records a decline in the relative representation of wild grasses when domesticated emmer becomes prominent around 9,800 cal BP. The authors consider the evidence insufficient to determine whether the earlier wild cereals were cultivated.

event.caveats: The domestication traits were recovered at Chogha Golan. Where they developed and whether the earlier wild cereals were cultivated locally remain unsettled.

date.label: Jiahu Period III (6200–5700 BCE)
date.basis: Cultural period of the measured fish remains in Fig. 1b, the period assigned to the inferred management. The abstract summarizes it as by around 6000 BCE.

event.statement: From the distribution of estimated fish sizes and the composition of fish remains, Nakajima and colleagues infer common carp management at Jiahu in Period III (6200–5700 BCE).

evidence.supports: was present at the Early Neolithic Jiahu site, Henan Province, China, by around 6000 bc
The authors infer fish management in Jiahu Period III (6200–5700 BCE), based on estimated body-length clusters and the proportion of common carp.

event.caveats: The measurements support an inference of management. The evidence leaves the location and form of the managed waters unresolved.

date.label: c. 5250–4650 cal BCE (Mehrgarh Period I context)
date.basis: Moulherat et al. placed grave MR.84.03.158 in Period I and used the then-current first-half sixth-millennium BCE estimate. Mutin et al. dated the Period I sequence to about 5250–4650 cal BCE from human teeth in the cemetery.

event.statement: Researchers identified cotton threads preserved within a copper bead from aceramic Neolithic grave MR.84.03.158 at Mehrgarh.

evidence.locator: pp. 1393–1396, Introduction and Description of the Beads, Figs. 2, 4, 7–9; pp. 1398–1400
evidence.supports: Identifies bead MR.84.03.158.01b and grave MR.84.03.158, assigns the burial to the aceramic Neolithic Period I and reports Gossypium threads.

evidence.locator: pp. 3–4, Fig. 2 and Discussion: The dating and duration of Mehrgarh Period I
evidence.supports: The newer cemetery model estimates about 5250–4650 cal BCE for Period I on the basis of enamel measurements on other archaeological material from the cemetery.

event.caveats: The range dates the Period I context. The bead and thread have no reported direct date, and grave 158 has not been securely matched to a dated tooth. No woven cloth survives in the bead.

date.label: Early Period, c. 6600–6400 cal BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: Dairy fats in pottery of the site's Early Period, which the paper dates to about 6600–6400 cal BCE, show that dairy products were already made and eaten at Barcın Höyük; the authors word this as 'by 6600 cal. BCE'.

evidence.supports: Barcın Höyük has shown that the production, transformation, and consumption of dairy products was already prevalent in Northwest Anatolia by 6600 cal. BCE, at the end of the first half of the seventh millennium cal. BCE (Early Period)

evidence.locator: Discussion, paragraphs on faunal remains and culling profiles
evidence.supports: The site had abundant domestic cattle and caprines. The authors infer mixed meat and milk use from sheep mortality and find no evidence of herd management that maximized milk production.

event.caveats: Early ceramics reflect processing of dairy products. The milk-producing species and the place where people learned the practice are unresolved.

date.label: Approximately 40,000 cal BP (38,050 BCE)
date.basis: Approximate archaeological context; calibrated BP values use 1950 as reference.

event.statement: An intact eyed bone needle was recovered in horizon 11.2 of the Main Chamber at Denisova Cave. The excavation team reported microscopic traces of wear.

evidence.supports: A 2024 archaeological review lists an eyed-needle date of approximately 40,000 cal BP at Denisova Cave.

evidence.locator: pp. 72–75, especially pp. 72–74 and Figs. 1–2 (same PDF pages)
evidence.supports: Records the needle’s exact chamber and horizon and describes polish and wear on the object. An estimated thread size is inferred from the eye.

event.caveats: The approximate age refers to the archaeological context. The 50,300 ± 2,200 radiocarbon-year determination elsewhere in the excavation report is from a cut-marked bone in the East Chamber. The needle's user, thread material and sewn product are unknown.

date.label: Approximately 11,300–11,200 cal BP (9350–9250 BCE)
date.basis: Authors estimate construction of Structure 4 phase I at approximately 11,300–11,200 cal BP, from stratigraphy and radiocarbon context; the conversion uses 1950 as BP reference.

event.statement: At Dhra in the Jordan Valley, a purpose-built structure interpreted as a granary had a suspended floor supported above ground, enabling food storage.
event.caveats: The floor and use are archaeological reconstructions; claims about ownership and storage duration are hypotheses. The date refers to phase I at one structure. Floor phytoliths and a flotation sample associated with the structure support the interpretation. The amount stored, the full contents and the date of the sampled deposit remain uncertain.

evidence.supports: Authors interpret Structure 4 as a raised-floor granary, with phase I construction approximately 11,300–11,200 cal BP.

evidence.locator: Dhra′ cereal densities, context 2134 and table 5
evidence.supports: A flotation sample from the layer between the floor and collapsed material in Structure 4 yielded charred barley grains at an above-average density for the site. The evidence concerns this sampled deposit associated with Structure 4.
The excavators reconstruct floor beams supported by stone uprights. Preliminary phytolith analysis found a concentration of barley husks in the mud floor.

date.label: around 3250 BCE
date.basis: Date or interval stated or closely scoped by the cited source; see event caveats.

event.statement: A British Museum educational account dates the development of Egyptian hieroglyphs to around 3250 BCE.
event.caveats: A retrospective estimate for the writing tradition. See the Tomb U-j event for the date and interpretation of a named archaeological witness.

evidence.supports: The museum dates development approximately and identifies hieroglyphs as Egyptian writing.

date.label: 3811–3640 cal BCE (reported wood-date components)
date.basis: Envelope of the two calibrated 2σ components reported for the wood samples, 3811–3710 BCE (63%) and 3810–3640 BCE (88.1%). The article summarises the age as about 3800–3700 BCE. The displayed envelope covers the reported components, which contain only part of each calibration’s probability.

event.statement: The surviving bent-birch frame and split-birch attachments from Gurgler Eisjoch are interpreted as a Late Neolithic snowshoe.
event.scope: A birch-branch hoop with crossing split-branch strands, interpreted as a framed snowshoe.
applications: Inferred travel over snow on an Alpine pass
event.population: Late Neolithic Alpine travelers associated with the Gurgler Eisjoch find
event.caveats: The measurements date the wood, which could predate construction or have been reused. Structure, wear and find context support the snowshoe interpretation. The exact tread, binding and date of a crossing remain uncertain.

evidence.supports: Describes the surviving frame, split strands and attached fragments, wear and impressions that helped reconstruct the positions of missing strands.

evidence.locator: p. 451, radiocarbon paragraph; p. 459, nn. 13–14; p. 462, summary
evidence.supports: Reports wood determinations of 5013 ± 23 and 4958 ± 45 radiocarbon years BP. Their reported calibrated 2σ components are 3811–3710 BCE (63%) and 3810–3640 BCE (88.1%). The article rounds the Late Neolithic age to about 3800–3700 BCE.

date.label: 120,000 to 90,000 years ago
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: The excavators read the carnivore bones with skinning marks and the bone tools likely used for fur processing, from the same deposits, as highly suggestive proxy evidence of clothing; the date range is that of the deposits, 120,000 to 90,000 years ago (about 118,050 to 88,050 BCE).

evidence.supports: The combination of carnivore bones with skinning marks and bone tools likely used for fur processing provide highly suggestive proxy evidence for the earliest clothing in the archaeological record.

evidence.locator: Results, pp. 3–6, Figs. 2–5 and Tables S2–S3
evidence.supports: Seven rib-bone spatulates are reported in Layer IV-2. The researchers compare their wear with hide-processing tools and distinguish the skinning marks on carnivore bones from marks on meat-processed bovids.

event.caveats: The layer-specific tools and cut-marked faunal assemblage support a hide and fur processing interpretation. The use of the prepared material for clothing is inferred.

date.label: c. 3200 BCE
date.basis: Closed burials assigned to Naqada IIC–IIIA, approximately 3400–3100 BCE; abstract rounds to 3200 BCE.

event.statement: Meteoritic iron hammered into sheet and rolled into tubular beads; a metalworking route requiring no extraction of iron from ore.
event.caveats: Rehren and colleagues infer intermittent annealing for the Petrie Museum samples. Johnson and colleagues identify traces of cold working in a different bead, Manchester Museum accession 5303. The complete thermal histories are uncertain.

evidence.locator: pp. 4785–4787: abstract, archaeological background, materials; pp. 4790–4791: discussion/conclusions
evidence.supports: Burial chronology, analyzed beads, meteoritic origin and sheet-rolling manufacture.
Analysis of a separate bead from Tomb 67 supports meteoritic iron, formation from a bent sheet, and cold working.

date.label: 2.6–2.5 million years ago
date.basis: Source reports geological age 2.6–2.5 Ma; calendar endpoints are rounded approximations and do not imply year-level precision.

event.statement: East Gona EG10 and EG12 stone artifacts are dated approximately 2.6–2.5 million years ago.

evidence.supports: Stone artifacts from the Gona sequence date approximately 2.6–2.5 million years ago.
The chapter dates EG10 and EG12 to 2.6–2.5 Ma, and describes sharp flakes, cores and fine-grained raw material selection.

evidence.locator: Introduction and site stratigraphy; Conjoining and refitting lithic sets from EG 10
evidence.supports: Identifies a probable local source of cobbles and reports physically refitted sets of flakes from East Gona 10.

contributions.group: Unidentified hominin toolmakers at East Gona

evidence.supports: Describes hominin manufacture of East Gona cores and flakes; species identity remains unknown.

event.scope: The dated event covers EG10 and EG12. The physical joins mentioned in the description were studied at EG10.

date.label: ca. 6000–5800 BC
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: The excavators and chemical analysts interpret residues in early Neolithic jars from Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora as evidence of likely grape wine at about 6000–5800 BCE.

evidence.locator: Archaeological Samples Chosen for Analysis, Pottery Prerequisites, Results and Discussion
evidence.supports: Reports organic acid detections compared with controls and attributes the jar residues to grape wine in view of local archaeological and environmental evidence.
Shows why tartaric acid alone cannot identify wine or its production.

date.label: more than 279,000 years ago (before c. 277,050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: Sahle and colleagues interpreted pointed obsidian artifacts from the Gademotta Formation as projectile points. The earliest context studied is older than 279,000 years.

evidence.supports: used as projectile weapons (in the form of hafted javelin tips) as early as >279,000 years ago
Separate geochemical study of a broad formation sample found most pieces match Worja obsidian. This result concerns assemblage provenance.

date.label: Approximately 6700–6400 years BP
date.basis: The paper reports individual combined ages of 6656–6450 BP and also summarizes the structures as about 6700–6500 years ago; rounded BCE endpoints cover both summaries using the conventional 1950 BP reference.

event.statement: Two stone structures at submerged Hishuley Carmel contained abundant olive stones. The excavators propose seawater or salt curing to explain the deposits. Modern experiments showed that olives could be fermented in seawater and that dry salting was also feasible.

evidence.supports: The paper compares relatively less-fragmented pits in Hishuley Carmel structures with highly fragmented pits at Kfar Samir and interprets them as evidence for preserved table olives; cultivation is unsettled.

evidence.locator: Results, experiment of olive fermentation in sea water and pickling olives with sea salt, Fig. 8; Discussion, function of the Hishuley Carmel structures
evidence.supports: The excavation context and fragmentation comparisons support the table-olive interpretation. A modern experiment tests seawater-based processing as a possible explanation.
The stone outlines resemble a range of presumed wild and modern cultivated forms without identifying an ancient source orchard.

event.caveats: Pickling or dry salting is an archaeological interpretation; the researchers cannot establish which method or whether the trees were cultivated.

date.label: c. 42,000 years ago (c. 40,050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: Jerimalai shelter in East Timor preserves fish remains, including scombrids, in its earliest dated occupation deposits.

evidence.supports: Reports the marine assemblage in Square B. The initial phase includes Scombridae identified at the family level.

evidence.locator: pp. 879–883 and O’Connor and Ono's reply
evidence.supports: Compares the local range of neritic and oceanic taxa. The presence of scombrids leaves capture zone and equipment unresolved.

event.caveats: In the 2011 analysis, Scombridae is a family-level identification. The bones do not by themselves identify where the fish were caught or whether people used boats or hooks.

date.label: c. 23,000–16,000 cal BP (c. 21,050–14,050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: A shell fishhook from Jerimalai shelter in Timor-Leste comes from a deposit dated between about 23,000 and 16,000 calibrated years before present (about 21,050–14,050 BCE).

evidence.supports: Another shell hook from Jerimalai Shelter in Timor-Leste is of a comparable age to the Okinawa find, in a deposit context dated to between c. 23000 and 16000 cal BP
Illustrates a broken shell fishhook and reports the stratigraphic age bracket of about 23–16 ka. The bracket dates associated sediment context.

date.label: about 6200 to 6000 years ago
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: Two weft-twined, blue-striped textiles were recovered from stratum 44. Chromatography on specimen 2009.052.01.B&C identified indigotin and indirubin in its blue yarn.

evidence.supports: The textile was made with plied warp yarns, including blue cotton stripes. Chromatography identified indigoid compounds on a yarn sample.
The dated contexts above and below stratum 44 provide a stratigraphic age estimate for the early indigo specimen.

evidence.locator: Fig. 12.1d and Color, Pigment, and Dye
evidence.supports: Illustrates the same inspected indigo specimen and identifies its excavation stratum.

event.scope: Production of indigo-striped cotton fabric, evidenced by the stratum 44 textile assemblage.
event.caveats: The age comes from stratum 44’s position between dated levels. The publications assign different phase labels to the specimen and agree on its stratum and identity.

date.label: Approximately 7000–5500 BCE, sampled Jiahu contexts
date.basis: The paper’s methods give sampled contexts from about 7000–5500 BCE while its note 10 gives the youngest period ending 5800 BCE; the wider reported interval preserves the discrepancy.

event.statement: Chemical residues in Jiahu pottery led McGovern and colleagues to infer a mixed fermented beverage of rice, honey and fruit.
event.caveats: Ingredients and fermentation are inferred from combined chemical and archaeological evidence; exact fruit and method remain uncertain. The methods and note 10 give conflicting youngest period endpoints (5500 versus 5800 BCE), so the wider span is retained; the individual positive sherds cannot be placed at one endpoint from this review.

evidence.supports: The authors analysed sherds from 16 vessels across Jiahu periods; methods and note 10 disagree on the youngest endpoint, and chemical evidence is interpreted as a mixed fermented beverage.

date.label: About 7500–7000 years BP
date.basis: The source gives approximately 7500–7000 BP for the site; the olive-oil assemblage itself is reported at approximately 7000 BP. Approximate BCE endpoints use 1950 as the BP reference.

event.statement: At submerged Kfar Samir, researchers found crushed olive stones and pulp in pits, including alternating layers of olive material and clay above a pebble base in pit 6. The excavators interpret these deposits as remains of oil extraction.

evidence.supports: The authors interpret crushed olives and installations at Kfar Samir (7500–7000 BP) as oil production and whole olives in structures at Hishuley Carmel (around 6600 BP) as preserved table olives. Both are archaeological interpretations; wild or cultivated trees are not settled.

evidence.locator: The archaeological findings and Discussion, Figs. 2 and 7
evidence.supports: Published excavation describes pit 6 and its olive remains, pulp and associated plant fragments.

event.caveats: The deposits support an oil-extraction interpretation. The use of individual installations, the role of particular baskets, and the fruit's wild or cultivated status remain uncertain.

date.label: Approximately 6950–6440 cal BP (5000–4490 BCE)
date.basis: Source-reported period or approximate chronology; where calibrated BP is stated, converted using the 1950 reference epoch.

event.statement: At Kuk Swamp in the New Guinea highlands, banana phytoliths occur in agricultural features and are interpreted as evidence for cultivation of Musa acuminata derivatives.
event.caveats: Cultivation is inferred from associated features and diagnostic plant remains, not a direct observation of planting; the chronology and species identifications remain subject to archaeological interpretation. The paper text gives 6950–6440 cal BP for the agricultural feature fills, while its figure caption gives 6990–6440 for one sample. A 2011 regional synthesis proposes complex domestication and possible westward dispersal, but does not trace a specific subsequent site to these individual Kuk remains.

evidence.supports: The authors date pertinent feature fills to 6950–6440 cal BP; rare phytoliths match M. acuminata and occur in an agricultural context.

evidence.locator: Bananas and conclusions, pp. S387–S388, S391
evidence.supports: The review describes a regionally complex history of banana domestication and cultivation inferred from phytoliths and features at Kuk. It discusses evidence suggestive of westward dispersal from the New Guinea region, while noting the lack of direct archaeobotanical verification for parts of the proposed route; no direct link from the individual Kuk assemblage is established.
Excavated Phase 2 surfaces date to 6950–6440 cal BP. The authors interpret the concentrations in early feature fills as evidence of bananas deliberately planted in mounded plots.
Reports elevated Musaceae phytolith frequencies and diagnostic Musa section seed phytoliths in samples from fills 3004 and 3009.

date.label: about 6,000 years ago (c. 4000 BCE)
date.basis: Thoury et al. describe an approximately 6000-year-old amulet and give 4500–3600 BCE for its find area.

event.statement: At Mehrgarh, a wheel-shaped copper amulet assigned an approximate age of 6000 years preserves evidence of lost-wax casting.

evidence.locator: Abstract, Fig. 1b and Results, ‘The Mehrgarh amulet is the earliest known lost-wax cast object’
evidence.supports: The study uses an approximate age of 6000 years, shows the 4500–3600 BCE find-area range, and analyses the amulet's original cast structure.

event.caveats: The age is approximate and contextual. The purity of the metal leaves native copper possible and the feedstock's origin unresolved.

date.label: 7600–7280 cal BP (c. 5650–5330 BCE)
date.basis: Roosevelt et al. Table 1 reports this 95% range for reduced carbon from sherd OxA-2431 in the base of level 12. The paper gives an older age for some associated charcoal and shell.

event.statement: A grit-tempered sherd from the base of level 12 in Test 1 yielded a reduced-carbon AMS date. Another piece of the same sherd yielded a much less precise thermoluminescence age.

evidence.supports: Table 1 identifies the dated sherd and carbon fractions. Table 2 and Fig. 5 show their excavation context.
Reports grit-tempered pottery, the TL assay on part of the same sherd, and possible dating biases.

event.place_note: Taperinha shell midden near Santarém, Pará
event.caveats: The two carbon fractions and the thermoluminescence measurement come from one sherd. The authors discuss potential contamination and uncertain environmental parameters.

date.label: c. 10,350 cal BP (c. 8400 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: The dated Isla Manechi profile contains a heart-shaped Manihot phytolith at approximately 10,350 cal BP. The authors interpret it as evidence of early cultivation.

evidence.locator: Evidence of early plant cultivation, Figs. 2–3
evidence.supports: Reports the Manihot phytolith from the dated Isla Manechi profile.

date.label: c. 10,250 cal BP (c. 8300 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: Dated Isla Manechi layers contain squash rind phytoliths at approximately 10,250 cal BP, with sizes in the domesticated range.

evidence.locator: Evidence of early plant cultivation, Fig. 3 and Extended Data Table 2
evidence.supports: Identifies the squash phytoliths and distinguishes their size from evidence of a local domestication trajectory.

date.label: 8200-7500 BC
date.basis: The 8200–7500 BCE interval is from Muşkara and Aydın's comparative table. The excavation report assigns individual objects to relative building subphases.

event.statement: Çayönü's Pre-Pottery Neolithic levels yielded worked native copper ornaments and small tools. The excavators place the first clear worked finds in the Grill Buildings and basal-pit contexts, and discuss metallographic indications of annealing in native copper.

evidence.supports: Çayönü 8200-7500 BC (Yalçın 2000) Anatolia, SE Native copper Malachite Annealing, coldworking

evidence.locator: pp. 15–19, distribution by building subphase and Figs. 1 and 4
evidence.supports: Early worked copper finds and later workshop areas are documented stratigraphically. The report identifies worked native copper separately from malachite and refers to metallographic indications of annealing.

event.caveats: The comparative dates serve as approximate context. A calibrated date for the first worked object and a secure geological source remain open.

date.label: 9600–8600 calibrated years BP
date.basis: Source date for the documented context; BP conversion uses 1950 as reference where applicable.

event.statement: A fish-rich pit at a forager settlement is interpreted as evidence for fermentation and storage of fish.

evidence.supports: Reports the fish-rich gutter, the concentration of cyprinids and vertebral alteration consistent with acid exposure, and interprets the assemblage as fermentation while considering other depositional explanations.

Norje Sunnansund is dated 9600–8600 calibrated BP; fish remains in a pit are interpreted as fermented and stored. The article reports 16,180 identified fish fragments across the site, not the catch size.

evidence.locator: Fish teeth data, figs. 8–11; Discussion and Concluding remarks
evidence.supports: Within-pit and outside-pit fish teeth differ in measured strontium isotope ratios. The authors infer autumn capture for the largely roach catch placed in the pit, using fish ecology and a local-baseline estimate.

event.caveats: The preservation technique and storage duration are inferred from context; the dates cover the site rather than a precisely dated individual production cycle.

contributions.resource: Norje Sunnansund fish fermentation and storage

evidence.supports: Norje Sunnansund is dated 9600–8600 calibrated BP; fish remains in a pit are interpreted as fermented and stored. The article reports 16,180 identified fish fragments across the site, not the catch size.

date.label: 3.032 to 2.581 million years ago
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: Oldowan sites at Nyayanga in south-western Kenya are dated to between 3.032 and 2.581 million years ago and show hippopotamus butchery and plant processing.

evidence.supports: The 3.032-2.581 Ma Oldowan sites from Nyayanga evidence hippo butchery, plant processing, and the first Paranthropus from SW Kenya.

evidence.locator: Results, Stone transport behavior and Figure 6; Discussion
evidence.supports: Multiple artifact classes indicate on-site tool manufacture, including the reduction of nonlocal stone.

event.scope: Nyayanga, Homa Peninsula, upper part of bed NY-1.

date.label: c. 7000 years ago (c. 5050 BCE)
date.basis: The approximate chronology of the two-species interpretation follows Langgut and Garfinkel (2022). Langgut (2024), Table 2, reports 7160–6950 cal BP for an olive branch and repeats 6960–6860 cal BP for a fig twig at 68.2% probability.

event.statement: Olive charcoal and young fig branches from Tel Tsaf are interpreted as evidence of local fruit-tree cultivation about 7000 years ago. Direct radiocarbon dates from Area C include a young olive branch and a fig twig.

evidence.supports: olive ( Olea europaea ) and fig ( Ficus carica ) horticulture was practiced as early as 7000 years ago in the Central Jordan Valley, Israel
Adds a direct 7160–6950 cal BP assay on the young olive branch Beta-657404. The fig twig Beta-585311 date was previously reported.

date.label: Before 9400 calibrated BCE
date.basis: Stratigraphic terminus ante quem, not an invention date.

event.statement: A bowl fragment and other ceramic sherds were redeposited in fluvial unit HA1 at Ravin de la Mouche before 9400 cal BCE, as bounded by the overlying dated deposits.

evidence.supports: Context chronology.

evidence.locator: pp. 909–911, HA1 formation and assemblage; Figs. 1 and 3
evidence.supports: The sherds are reworked material in stratified unit HA1. The overlying dated deposits give a terminus ante quem for redeposition.

date.label: 12,130–11,080 cal BP across dated specimens
date.basis: The quoted interval spans the oldest and youngest boundaries of the early fibre determinations in Jolie et al. Table 2. Individual specimen intervals are separate.

event.statement: A two-ply cord dates to 12,130–11,800 cal BP. Closely and openly twined fragments date to 11,330–11,100 and 11,280–11,080 cal BP respectively.

evidence.supports: Direct determinations distinguish the early two-ply cord and close and open twining from a much later spiral-interlinked fragment.
The article describes the textile structures, constituent fibres and possible uses and reports fibre coils among the excavated material.

event.caveats: Direct dates apply to the sampled cords and fabrics. The tested spiral-interlinked fragment was much younger. Clothing, containers and matting are interpretations of fragment form and wear.

date.label: around 3900–3800 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: Archaeological evidence indicates that wheel-coiling was adopted in northern Mesopotamia in the early 4th millennium BCE, around 3900 to 3800 BCE.

evidence.supports: chronological coincidence with northern Mesopotamia – supported by archaeological evidence (Baldi, 2013; Vallet et al., 2017) indicating an adoption of wheel-coiling in the early 4th millennium (around 3900–3800 BCE)

evidence.locator: Tell Feres case study and Figs. 2–4
evidence.supports: Excavated northern Mesopotamian bowls in later LC2 strata show microstructural coil joints and rotation marks.

date.label: around 7000 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: Nieuwenhuyse concluded that the ceramics in the earliest pottery layers at Tell Sabi Abyad and Shir, dating to around 7000 BCE, were not necessarily the result of earlier local experiments.

evidence.supports: dating to around 7000 BCE, were not necessarily the result of experiments that took place at older, yet-to-be discovered
evidence.locator: Chapter 2, Spoor, A Man Feasting. Olivier's Journey through Archaeology

evidence.supports: Original excavation series documents the early Tell Sabi Abyad stratigraphic and ceramic observations.

date.label: About 75,000 years ago
date.basis: The primary abstract reports archaeological levels of approximately 75 ka; the coordinate is an approximate conversion, not an exact event year.

event.statement: At Blombos, archaeological points show a separately inferred use of pressure flaking in their final shaping.
event.scope: Pressure flaking interpreted in the final shaping of heat-treated silcrete Still Bay points.
event.caveats: The original full research paper was not accessible for retention; the inspected original abstract and later Sibudu paper are used.
