Ancestry or direct transfer from Sibudu is not established. Ochre objects provide a separate witness to pressure flaking in the Still Bay occupation. The studies do not match an ochre tool to a particular finished object.

evidence.supports: The research abstract attributes final shaping of Still Bay silcrete points in ~75 ka levels to pressure flaking.
Independently contrasts Blombos final shaping with the Sibudu notching interpretation.

evidence.locator: The ochre retouchers; Results, Table 1 and Figure 3
evidence.supports: Two ochre objects from Still Bay layers independently preserve wear interpreted as pressure flaking on stone. The archaeological series are distinct.

date.label: over 30,000 years ago (before c. 28,050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: The Australian Museum attributes food processing residues to a sandstone grindstone fragment from Cuddie Springs and reports an age over 30,000 years for its context.

evidence.supports: found in the Cuddie Springs archaeological site, on Wailwan Country, demonstrates the longevity of food preparation dating back over 30,000 years

An independent dating study disputes a single interpretation in which all SU6 sediments, artefacts and animal remains were deposited together at the luminescence ages. The analyses concern fauna and its context.

event.caveats: The museum's age is contextual. Analyses of faunal remains from Cuddie Springs complicate the site's chronology, without directly dating this grinding fragment.

date.label: c. 164,000 years ago (±12,000)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: The LC-MSA Lower at Pinnacle Point Cave 13B preserves an assemblage of marine shells interpreted as food remains, dated to about 164,000 ± 12,000 years ago.

evidence.supports: Reports luminescence dating of the lower deposit and identifies Perna perna as the most abundant shellfish by minimum number of individuals in that layer. Uses living shellfish habitats to infer intertidal collection.

date.label: Approximately 5,000 cal BP (3050 BCE)
date.basis: Lee and colleagues’ approximate age of the Mid-Jomon find, based on directly dated charred Glycine seed PLD-9088 and the midden context.

event.statement: Large soybean seeds at Shimoyakebe are interpreted as evidence consistent with human selection.

evidence.supports: The researchers compare soybean seed sizes and identify large Middle Jomon specimens at Shimoyakebe around 5,000 calibrated years before 1950, interpreting enlargement as evidence consistent with selection. Size is an imperfect proxy for domestication, and the finding does not establish a single point of origin.

evidence.locator: Table 1, sample SY 37 (PLD-9088); English summary p. 26
evidence.supports: Original report of the directly dated charred Glycine seed from the Middle Jomon walnut midden. It documents the same dated specimen cited by Lee and colleagues.

event.caveats: The approximate date summarizes a Middle Jomon assemblage; the study reports an AMS date directly on a charred soybean and notes agreement with other material. Seed size alone cannot prove domestication, cultivation or unique origin; selection is the authors’ inference.

date.label: c. 3550 to 3350 BCE (5,500 to 5,300 years ago)
date.basis: Approximate age range reported in the 2019 Xinhua account. The museum’s W12 laboratory note identifies the fabric and does not give a direct date.

event.statement: The China National Silk Museum identified carbonised crossed-warp fabric from urn W12 at Wanggou as silk.

evidence.locator: pp. 44–45 (PDF p. 32), testing of residues from the Wanggou urn burials
evidence.supports: Reports plain-weave and finer crossed-warp material in W12 and identifies the crossed-warp fabric as silk with ELISA.
The silk fabrics at the Wanggou date back between 5,300 and 5,500 years.
evidence.locator: Paragraph on dating, after the ELISA identification

event.caveats: The W12 test identifies silk in the crossed-warp material. The age in the press account is contextual. The specimen establishes cloth in the burial; the place of its manufacture and the way the silk was obtained remain open.

date.label: Middle Pastoral contexts approximately 5210–3660 BCE
date.basis: The 2018 review reports the Middle Pastoral Takarkori range as 5210–3660 BCE in Table 1; pottery lipid interpretations are context-associated.

event.statement: Food residues and animal remains at Takarkori rock shelter support a pastoral system that included processing milk products.

evidence.supports: The review gives Middle Pastoral context 5210–3660 BCE and discusses dairy residues and cattle remains.
Original compound-specific carbon isotope measurements distinguish ruminant dairy fat in selected Middle Pastoral potsherds.

event.caveats: Lipid residues identify ruminant dairy and are dated by the pottery context. The species that provided milk and how it was processed remain open.

date.label: early PPNB, 8500–8000 cal BCE
date.basis: The chart range is the Early PPNB comparison bin in Arbuckle and Kassebaum’s Table 1. Helmer et al. assign the Dja’de samples to 8800–8300 cal BCE in their own chronology.

event.statement: A review reports Helmer's argument that cattle at Dja'de al-Mughara, a site of the early PPNB (8500–8000 calibrated BC in the review's Table 1), are the first to show domestic form; the review itself regards the size change as small and contested.

evidence.supports: Dramatic changes in human cattle relationships are reflected at the site of Dja’de al-Mughara dating to the early PPNB ( EPPNB ), where Helmer argues morphologically domestic cattle are evident for the first time
Original measurements suggest that male bone dimensions changed more strongly than female dimensions; the authors infer early domestication at Dja’de.

event.caveats: The size changes differ by skeletal element and the sample may include hunted aurochs. The chart range is the review’s Early PPNB bin, while the original study used an older assemblage chronology.

date.label: Layer IV, modeled between 6.4–6.0 and 5.8–4.5 ka BP
date.basis: The deposit phase has separate age intervals for its onset and end. The outer bounds here use the oldest and youngest limits of the Le Neün et al. phase estimates, converted from cal BP using the 1950 convention.

event.statement: Layer IV at Telarmachay contains vicuña-like ankle bones with a distinct joint shape. Researchers interpret the change as possible intensification of management affecting camelid movement.
event.caveats: Possible management is inferred from morphology and mortality. The original excavators interpreted human confinement and domestication, while the later comparison permits less restrictive herding and does not identify fully domestic phenotypes.

evidence.supports: Compares layer IV with earlier layers and interprets shape change as stronger management of camelid mobility.
Isotope measurements indicate relatively stable camelid diets and environments across the layers analysed.

evidence.locator: pp. 275–281, De la chasse à la domestication
evidence.supports: Original excavation synthesis reports elevated neonatal mortality and alpaca-like incisor forms and interprets these as early domestication.
The authors report Wheeler’s proposal of management by approximately 6000 calibrated BP, based on faunal age and dental morphology.

date.label: Approximately 8200–7500 cal BCE (Middle PPNB, phase AW2)
date.basis: Douché and Willcox’s table 1 gives the approximate calendar interval of archaeological phase AW2.

event.statement: In Tell Aswad’s phase AW2, domestic-type, non-shattering forms constitute a substantial share of the identified barley spikelet bases. Wild-type remains still predominate.

evidence.supports: Using secure Pre-Pottery Neolithic B contexts and a revised stratigraphy, the authors report that domestic-type barley spikelet bases first form a substantial share in phase AW2. Table 1 dates AW2 to approximately 8200–7500 cal BCE.

event.caveats: The date refers to the phase yielding the remains. The revised study places the first substantial representation of this trait at Tell Aswad in AW2. The time and place where domestication began remain uncertain.

date.label: c. 4300-4000 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

event.statement: Two sites east of Lake Tai, of the Late Majiabang period dated 4300-4000 BCE, have produced evidence of ancient field systems.

evidence.supports: Two sites east of Taihu Lake of the Late Majiabang cultural period (4300–4000) have produced evidence for ancient field systems
evidence.locator: Section 'Yangzte pre-domestication cultivation and early paddy-fields', p. 95
pp. 164–169, Table 1, Fig. 2 and Table 2; p. 172 conclusions
evidence.supports: Caoxieshan pit samples and features support a local shift from use of a natural depression to artificial pits with ditches and furrows. The authors associate the shift with falling local water levels.

date.label: About 1.0 or 0.75 million years ago
date.basis: Berna et al. preferred the Jaramillo correlation at about 1.0 Ma. Marin-Monfort et al. list the Jaramillo and early Brunhes as competing correlations, at about 1.0 and 0.75 Ma respectively. The chart bounds enclose two alternative estimates and imply no continuous measured interval.

event.statement: Burned bone and ashed plant remains occur in early hominin occupation sediments inside Wonderwerk Cave.
event.caveats: Hominin involvement in burning is an archaeological inference, and the study did not identify constructed hearths; age and fire control are debated.

evidence.supports: Researchers report in situ burned materials in the early Acheulean occupation.
Identifies Stratum 10 with lithostratigraphic unit 4a and reports alternative age correlations around 0.75 or 1.0 Ma.
Adds positive evidence for burning from a small mammal fossil sample within Stratum 10.

date.label: 20,000–19,000 calibrated years BP
date.basis: Source dates archaeological contexts in calibrated years before present; 1950 is the BP reference.

event.statement: Earliest pottery-bearing contexts are dated 20,000–19,000 calibrated years BP. The earliest West Area sherds include slab-built vessels, some with parallel scrape marks.

evidence.supports: The earliest pottery-bearing contexts are dated 20,000–19,000 calibrated years BP.
Summarises forming observations for early slab-built sherds, and distinguishes later coiling and paddling at the cave.

contributions.group: Mobile foragers associated with Xianrendong Cave

evidence.supports: Authors attribute the early cave pottery to mobile foragers.

date.label: Proposed c. 6050 BCE (chronology disputed)
date.basis: Chen et al. cite archaeology for approximately 8000 years before present. Mutin et al. subsequently proposed a later chronology for the aceramic cemetery at Mehrgarh.

event.statement: A genome study, citing archaeological evidence, places domesticated indicine cattle in the Indus Valley at about 8000 years before present (c. 6050 BCE, counting from 1950).

evidence.supports: Archaeological evidence indicates the presence of domesticated indicine cattle earlier in the Indus Valley (~8000 YBP) than in South India (~5000 YBP) and the middle Ganges (~4000 YBP)

evidence.locator: pp. 90–94, Figs. 7.1–7.2 and text on Bos
evidence.supports: Primary bone measurements show changing cattle size distributions across the archaeological sequence at Mehrgarh.

evidence.locator: Abstract; pp. 3–4, Fig. 2 and Discussion, The dating and duration of Mehrgarh Period I
evidence.supports: The new model dates the start of the human cemetery to 5200–4900 BCE and challenges the earlier site chronology used to contextualize cattle remains.

event.caveats: The approximately 6050 BCE estimate comes from the archaeology cited by Chen et al. New dates for the cemetery concern human enamel. Direct dating of taxonomically diagnostic cattle remains remains necessary to settle the earliest evidence.

dreyer-2011-abydos-tomb-uj.title: Tomb U-j: A Royal Burial of Dynasty 0 at Abydos
dreyer-2011-abydos-tomb-uj.version: Before the Pyramids: The Origins of Egyptian Civilization, Oriental Institute Museum Publications 33, pp. 127–136

passages.note: Ceramic phase is Naqada IIIa2. The excavator dates the tomb about 150 years before the First Dynasty, whose beginning he places circa 3200–3150 BCE.
Reports incised bone and ivory tags with holes and separate ink-marked vessels. Reads several tag signs as phonetic and interprets the tags as labels.

goldwasser-2006-egyptian-sign-models.title: Canaanites Reading Hieroglyphs: Horus is Hathor? The Invention of the Alphabet in Sinai
goldwasser-2006-egyptian-sign-models.version: Egypt and the Levant 16, 121–160, author-hosted PDF

passages.note: The author compares Egyptian sign models and early alphabetic signs. For consonant ʿayin, she compares the Egyptian eye (D4) with examples from Sinai 352, 375a and 346 and considers other sources for some variants.

gorsdorf-dreyer-hartung-1998-abydos-radi.title: New ¹⁴C Dating of the Archaic Royal Necropolis Umm el-Qaab at Abydos (Egypt)

passages.note: Reports incised tags in U-j, calibrated ranges for two wood samples from chamber 6 and a modeled phase estimate for Naqada IIIa2 near the middle of the 34th century BCE.

hoflmayer-2021-lachish-alphabet.title: Early alphabetic writing in the ancient Near East: the ‘missing link’ from Tel Lachish

passages.locator: pp. 711–714, especially Fig. 7 and first-line reading
passages.note: Independent excavation of a later rim sherd with a readable eye-shaped consonant ʿayin. The authors compare it with Egyptian eye D4 and discuss other signs and plausible chronological differences.

johnson-2013-gerzeh-iron-bead.title: Analysis of a prehistoric Egyptian iron bead with implications for the use and perception of meteorite iron in ancient Egypt

passages.note: Microscopy and micro-CT of Manchester Museum accession 5303 from Gerzeh Tomb 67 support meteoritic origin and a bent sheet seam. The authors interpret retained distorted taenite bands as cold working.

ozdogan-1999-early-metallurgy-cayonu.title: Archaeological evidence on the early metallurgy at Çayönü Tepesi
ozdogan-1999-early-metallurgy-cayonu.version: The Beginnings of Metallurgy, Der Anschnitt Beiheft 9, pp. 13–22
ozdogan-1999-early-metallurgy-cayonu.lineage: Excavators' published report inspected as a printed facsimile. The archaeological inventory is original and its discussion of annealing draws on earlier metallographic studies on site finds.

passages.locator: pp. 15–16, sequence and distribution of finds
passages.note: Unworked malachite is reported from Round Buildings deposits. Worked native copper and worked malachite first occur clearly in Grill Buildings and basal pits. Later workshop-area finds include blanks, finished ornaments and stone, bone and obsidian tools.

passages.locator: pp. 16–19, distribution table and Figs. 1 and 4
passages.note: The finds are inventoried by building subphase and separately counted as worked copper, worked malachite and raw malachite. Figure 4 shows a rolled worked copper bead. The report cites metallography for indications of annealing.

parker-2022-serabit-chronology.title: The Proto-Sinaitic Inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim in Their Archaeological Context: Date and Function
parker-2022-serabit-chronology.version: Egypt and the Levant 32, pp. 269–311, author copy

passages.note: A contextual reassessment argues for alphabetic writing locally circa 1850–1800 BCE. Identifies the sphinx with the reign of Senwosret III on stylistic and contextual grounds.

tallet-2014-wadi-el-jarf-papyri.title: Des papyrus du temps de Chéops au ouadi el-Jarf (golfe de Suez)
tallet-2014-wadi-el-jarf-papyri.version: Bulletin de la Société française d’égyptologie 188, pp. 25–49, DOI 10.3406/bsfe.2014.1208

passages.note: The excavator places Khufu’s reign approximately in 2550–2520 BCE.

tallet-2017-merer-logbooks-extract.title: Les papyrus de la mer Rouge I. Le « journal de Merer » (Papyrus Jarf A et B)
tallet-2017-merer-logbooks-extract.version: IFAO MIFAO 136, publisher extract with English Annex I translated by Colin Clement, ISBN 978-2-7247-0706-9

passages.locator: PDF pp. 2, 5–8, 16 (cover summary and Annex I)
passages.note: The edition identifies the A and B fragments as two hieratic logbooks from late in Khufu’s reign. The translation preserves daily entries about Inspector Merer’s team.

verhoeven-2023-hieratic.title: Hieratic
verhoeven-2023-hieratic.version: UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology, version 1 (June 2024 correction), DOI 10.5070/G9.4138

passages.locator: Abstract and pp. 4–5, Sources and Contexts of Inked Hieratic, Fig. 1
passages.note: Describes hieratic as a cursive form of the Egyptian hieroglyphic system, identifies Merer’s Fourth-Dynasty surviving log sheets and discusses fragment BIV alongside its photograph.

wilson-wright-2013-sinai-345.title: Interpreting the Sinaitic Inscriptions in Context: A New Reading of Sinai 345
wilson-wright-2013-sinai-345.version: Hebrew Bible and Ancient Israel 2(2), pp. 136–148, author offprint

passages.note: Describes Egyptian and early alphabetic texts on Sinai 345, compares the Northwest Semitic dedication with the Egyptian Hathor reference and reassesses the harder-to-read alphabetical text from the earlier photographs.

de-lumley-2018-east-gona-refits.title: The first technical sequences in human evolution from East Gona, Afar region, Ethiopia
de-lumley-2018-east-gona-refits.lineage: Primary refitting analysis of the existing East Gona 10 assemblage. Some excavators and material overlap with the earlier Gona studies. Source-gravel selection discussion uses earlier geological research, while refitting provides a new object-level observation.

passages.locator: Introduction and site stratigraphy; Conjoining and refitting lithic sets from EG 10
passages.note: The artifacts overlie an intermediate cobble conglomerate regarded as a probable raw material source. East Gona 10 includes trachyte and rhyolite cobbles with relatively few visible crystals. Physical joins among flakes include seven knapping sets, one of 14 pieces, which the authors interpret as evidence of sequential working of individual cobbles.

file.method: Short attributed paraphrases of the inspected passages. No original article bytes are retained.

finestone-2025-nyayanga-stone-transport.title: Selective use of distant stone resources by the earliest Oldowan toolmakers
finestone-2025-nyayanga-stone-transport.version: Science Advances 11(33), eadu5838, DOI 10.1126/sciadv.adu5838, PMC full text rendering.
finestone-2025-nyayanga-stone-transport.lineage: Primary comparison of the chemistry and composition of artifacts and geological source samples. Shares Nyayanga contributors and archaeological material with Plummer et al. (2023), whose field stratigraphy and tool observations are separate evidence. Some source data build on previous surveys. The new study samples more deposits and makes a new artifact-to-source comparison.

passages.locator: Results, Sources accessed by hominins and Stone transport distance, Figures 4–5
passages.note: The sampled local conglomerates lack suitable naturally occurring Bukoban quartzite; quartzite artifacts most closely match the Oboro source samples in the Awach Tende drainage about 13 km away. Younger eastern conglomerates are geological analogues for older sources, and the precise ancient pickup location remains unknown.

passages.locator: Results, Stone transport behavior and Figure 6; Discussion
passages.note: Nonlocal raw materials account for most of the assemblage mass. Outer surfaces on flakes and cores and other reduction indicators support transport of relatively little-worked raw material and on-site work. The study interprets probable travels exceeding 10 km; it does not directly observe a route or purpose.

The study assigns the NY-1 archaeological context a bracket of 3.040–2.581 Ma. The 2023 field report uses 3.032 Ma for the older bound in its final summary. The artifact deposits supply the date, with no direct date of stone collection.

file.method: Short attributed paraphrases of the inspected passages. No original article bytes are retained.

marin-monfort-2026-wonderwerk-strata-10-.title: New evidence for Early Pleistocene use of fire at Wonderwerk Cave (South Africa)
marin-monfort-2026-wonderwerk-strata-10-.version: PLOS One 21(6), e0347480, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0347480, PMC full text rendering.
marin-monfort-2026-wonderwerk-strata-10-.lineage: Primary analyses of small mammal fossils from Beaumont's Wonderwerk excavations, including a previously studied taphonomic collection. Berna et al. (2012) and this paper share site investigators. The new analyses largely concern a different material sample from the earlier micromorphological study, and the methods within this study assay some of the same fossils.

passages.note: Excavation 1 Stratum 11 sample is from lithostratigraphic unit 7 at the base of a reversed-polarity interval, bracketed by the Olduvai and Jaramillo subchrons at 1.79–1.07 Ma. The authors discuss a possible age nearer the older bound without resolving it. Stratum 10, unit 4a, is listed with two possible age correlations, approximately 0.75 or 1.0 Ma.

Some small mammal fossils in Strata 10 and 11 carry signatures of heating under infrared spectroscopy and luminescence. Both analyses agree on the 32 selected white or grey Stratum 11 samples. They are part of a targeted sample of 42 fossils from that stratum, not a prevalence estimate. The authors interpret localized burning deep within the cave in an occupation context as evidence consistent with fire brought in by hominins.

mazza-2006-campitello-birch-tar.title: A new Palaeolithic discovery: tar-hafted stone tools in a European Mid-Pleistocene bone-bearing bed
mazza-2006-campitello-birch-tar.version: Journal of Archaeological Science 33(9), pp. 1310–1318, DOI 10.1016/j.jas.2006.01.006. Published article read in indexed text rendering.
mazza-2006-campitello-birch-tar.lineage: Primary excavation report with chemical analyses of residues. The 2019 comparison refers back to these same two objects for Campitello, and independently analyzes an artifact from the Dutch North Sea.

passages.note: Two flakes bear residue at the quarry. One was found near the elephant remains and the other beneath a rib. Dating is based on geological context and associated fauna. The authors place the finds in the late Middle Pleistocene and infer a cold interval before oxygen isotope stage 6.
Infrared spectroscopy and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry were used to characterize the preserved residue. The authors identify triterpenoids consistent with birch tar.

shackley-sahle-2017-gademotta-obsidian.version: Geoarchaeology 32(2), pp. 302–310, DOI 10.1002/gea.21579, first published online 2016. Author-uploaded text read.
shackley-sahle-2017-gademotta-obsidian.lineage: Primary X-ray fluorescence comparison of archaeological obsidian and geological samples. Shares Sahle with the 2013 artifact study. velliky-2025-blombos-ochre-retouchers.title: Unveiling the multifunctional use of ochre in the Middle Stone Age: Specialized ochre retouchers from Blombos Cave
velliky-2025-blombos-ochre-retouchers.version: Science Advances 11(26), eads2797, DOI 10.1126/sciadv.ads2797, PMC full text rendering.
velliky-2025-blombos-ochre-retouchers.lineage: Primary analysis of ochre artifacts. Mourre et al. (2010) describe a different object class, silcrete artifacts, and share one author, Christopher S. Henshilwood. The archaeological specimens were never paired across the studies.

passages.note: The age estimates are of the archaeological phases. Still Bay phases M1 and M2 upper are dated to approximately 77–73 ka BP. The authors also discuss pre–Still Bay pieces, with alternative age descriptions depending on context or dating method.

passages.locator: The ochre retouchers; Results, Table 1 and Figure 3
passages.note: The authors interpret wear on Still Bay ochre specimens CB.200 and CFB-CFC.1566 as consistent with pressure flaking. The study reports seven ochre retoucher specimens in total, including pieces in earlier deposits, some with wear also interpreted as consistent with pressure flaking. It notes that pressure-flaked products have not yet been identified in the studied pre–Still Bay sample.

yellen-1995-katanda-worked-bone.title: A middle stone age worked bone industry from Katanda, Upper Semliki Valley, Zaire
yellen-1995-katanda-worked-bone.version: Science 268(5210), pp. 553–556, DOI 10.1126/science.7725100, original abstract via PubMed.
yellen-1995-katanda-worked-bone.lineage: Primary excavation synthesis of three Katanda sites. Its approximate age is part of the original excavators' interpretation. Brooks et al. (1995) is a companion dating report for the same sites, and later assessments retain a broader chronology.

passages.note: Reports both barbed and unbarbed worked bone points in a Middle Stone Age context and fish remains at Katanda. The authors propose an age around 90,000 years or older. The abstract does not resolve specimen-level dates, preserved attachments or use.

china-national-silk-museum-2017-wanggou-.title: Testing of residues excavated from Wanggou urn burials, Zhengzhou
china-national-silk-museum-2017-wanggou-.version: China National Silk Museum 2017 annual report, pp. 44–45. Section 郑州汪沟遗址出土瓮棺残留物测试.
china-national-silk-museum-2017-wanggou-.lineage: Original museum laboratory reporting on the Wanggou urn samples. The 2019 Xinhua account reports the museum and excavation team's findings, so it is not independent identification of the silk.

passages.locator: pp. 44–45 (PDF p. 32), testing of residues from the Wanggou urn burials
passages.note: The team examined fifteen samples from W12 and W20 together. Carbonised fabric in W12 showed two structures, a coarser plain weave and a finer crossed-warp weave tentatively described as leno. The ELISA result identifies the latter as silk. The report does not provide the calibrated date of W12.

derevianko-2016-denisova-main-chamber-ne.title: Early Upper Paleolithic Bone Needle from the Main Chamber of Denisova Cave (Based on Research Data from the 2016 Excavations)
derevianko-2016-denisova-main-chamber-ne.version: Problemy arkheologii, etnografii, antropologii Sibiri i sopredelnykh territorii XXII, 72–75. Institute of Archaeology and Ethnography, Siberian Branch, Russian Academy of Sciences. Russian original with English abstract.
derevianko-2016-denisova-main-chamber-ne.lineage: Original excavation and use-wear report. The excavator's 2025 article reproduces the same needle image and is not a new specimen. The dates cited for site layers are contextual and the 50,300 ± 2200 BP measurement is from a cut-marked bone in the East Chamber.

passages.locator: pp. 72–75, especially pp. 72–74 and Figs. 1–2 (same PDF pages)
passages.note: The complete eyed bone needle came from Main Chamber lithological horizon 11.2. Microscopy found polish and other use traces; the authors infer use of a fine thread from the eye, but no thread survived with this artefact. They report a lower-limit radiocarbon result for the middle of Main Chamber layer 11, separate from the dated bone in the East Chamber.

kaaronen-2025-antrea-knot-analysis.title: The Ties That Bind: Computational, Cross-cultural Analyses of Knots Reveal Their Cultural Evolutionary History and Significance
kaaronen-2025-antrea-knot-analysis.lineage: Independent topological analysis using archaeological knot descriptions and illustrations, including Pälsi's Antrea evidence. This is a new interpretation of published knot data, not new excavation or direct dating.

passages.locator: pp. 479–481, Discussion: Cultural transmission, task differentiation, and the deep past of knots; Fig. 1E
passages.note: Classifies the published Antrea knot as a sheet bend in an alternative orientation and compares similarly classified knots at Zamostje-2, Vis-1 and Satrup. The authors leave open transmission versus convergence. Their reported Antrea age of 10,522 cal BP cites Manninen et al., rather than a new radiocarbon test.

moulherat-2002-first-evidence-cotton.title: First Evidence of Cotton at Neolithic Mehrgarh, Pakistan: Analysis of Mineralized Fibres from a Copper Bead
moulherat-2002-first-evidence-cotton.version: Journal of Archaeological Science 29(12), 1393–1401. DOI 10.1006/jasc.2001.0779. Original article as served in the web PDF reader.
moulherat-2002-first-evidence-cotton.lineage: The deposited journal article is the primary analysis. The previously cited Harappa.com summary reports the same specimen and study.

passages.locator: pp. 1393–1396, Introduction and Description of the Beads, Figs. 2, 4, 7–9; pp. 1398–1400
passages.note: The original article identifies grave MR.84.03.158 and copper bead MR.84.03.158.01b as Period I and reports the then-current estimate of the first half of the sixth millennium BCE. Reflected-light microscopy and SEM identified mineralised threads as Gossypium sp. Morphology does not distinguish a particular modern species or domesticated stock. Copper corrosion preserved the threads.

mutin-2025-mehrgarh-period-i-radiocarbon.title: New radiocarbon dates of human tooth enamel reveal a late appearance of farming life in the Indus Valley
mutin-2025-mehrgarh-period-i-radiocarbon.lineage: New radiocarbon measurements on human dental enamel from the Period I cemetery and a Bayesian analysis. The tooth samples are independent of the material examined by Moulherat and colleagues.

passages.locator: pp. 3–4, Fig. 2 and Discussion: The dating and duration of Mehrgarh Period I
passages.note: The reported revised envelope for Period I is 5250–4650 cal BCE. The model separately estimates a cemetery onset of 5223–4914 cal BCE and end of 4769–4679 cal BCE. The grain of those estimates is the cemetery sequence. No match to grave MR.84.03.158 was identified in the published Figure 2.

steiner-2016-ein-jungsteinzeitlicher-sch.title: Ein jungsteinzeitlicher Schneereif vom Gurgler Eisjoch (3134 m) im Pfossental/Schnals (Südtirol)
steiner-2016-ein-jungsteinzeitlicher-sch.version: Archäologisches Korrespondenzblatt 46(4), pp. 445–463. DOI 10.11588/ak.2016.4.74815. Full original article text as displayed by Academia.edu; journal online issue posted in 2020.
steiner-2016-ein-jungsteinzeitlicher-sch.lineage: The version read reproduces the original report. The journal abstract and museum description summarize the same artefact. Two measurements from separate laboratories concern the same physical object.

passages.note: The authors identify birch wood, describe the hoop and crossing split branches, and distinguish surviving pieces and attachment traces from a reconstructed original arrangement. They describe signs of wear on the hoop and interpret use as a snowshoe.

passages.locator: p. 451, radiocarbon paragraph; p. 459, nn. 13–14; p. 462, summary
passages.note: The article reports 5013 ± 23 BP, with a stated 2σ component 3811–3710 BCE (63%), and 4958 ± 45 BP, with a stated 2σ component 3810–3640 BCE (88.1%). It summarises the object's Late Neolithic date as 3800–3700 BCE. Laboratory identifiers in nn. 13 and 14 are D37/15-DSH7145_W and LTL16459A. The measurements date wood.

bocquentin-nous-2022-natufian-phases.title: Considerations on the mechanisms of integration of the dead in the early sedentary societies of the Near East (Natufian, 15-11.6 ka cal BP)
bocquentin-nous-2022-natufian-phases.version: Bulletins et mémoires de la Société d’Anthropologie de Paris 34(1), pp. 15–28
bocquentin-nous-2022-natufian-phases.lineage: Published text read in its OpenEdition PDF rendering. Used for the early phase chronology.

passages.note: The regional Early Natufian range is given as 13–11.6 ka cal BC. The period range provides chronological context for Shelter 1 and does not directly date any plaster sample.

haklay-gopher-2015-eynan-shelters.title: A New Look at Shelter 131/51 in the Natufian Site of Eynan (Ain-Mallaha), Israel
haklay-gopher-2015-eynan-shelters.lineage: Original analysis of the early settlement's architecture using excavation plans and stratigraphy. Shelter 1 is contextual evidence from the excavations discussed in the paper. Kingery and colleagues separately analysed the material.

passages.locator: The Early Natufian architectural remains, fig. 1
passages.note: The authors describe a lime-plastered bench in Early Natufian Shelter 1 (Layer II). They note differing suggested functions for the shelter and distinguish it from Shelter 131/51.

hodder-2003-catalhoyuk-building-3-door.title: Introduction
hodder-2003-catalhoyuk-building-3-door.lineage: Project director’s season report on the Building 3: BACH team’s excavation. Building 3 supplies a separate instance from Matthews’s Building 1.

passages.note: The team found a blocked doorway behind plaster when removing the walls and examining the foundations. The report interprets it as evidence for ground-level entry in at least some phases.

kingery-1988-eynan-lime-plaster.title: The Beginnings of Pyrotechnology, Part II: Production and Use of Lime and Gypsum Plaster in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic Near East

peltenburg-2003-mylouthkia-well-116.title: Conclusions: Mylouthkia 1 and the Early Colonists of Cyprus
peltenburg-2003-mylouthkia-well-116.version: In The Colonisation and Settlement of Cyprus: Investigations at Kissonerga-Mylouthkia, 1976–1996
peltenburg-2003-mylouthkia-well-116.lineage: Excavator’s chapter in the final project report, inspected as a digital transcription of the printed volume.

abell-2019-asikli-urine-salts.title: Urine salts elucidate Early Neolithic animal management at Aşıklı Höyük, Turkey
abell-2019-asikli-urine-salts.version: Science Advances 5, eaaw0038. Author list abbreviated.
abell-2019-asikli-urine-salts.lineage: Primary soil and sediment chemistry from the site, a different set of measurements than the zooarchaeological counts and ages. Some excavation-team authors overlap.

passages.note: Levels 5–4 date to approximately 10,400–10,000 cal BP. Modelled human-and-animal inputs of urine salts rise markedly through the occupational sequence.

di-lernia-2021-takarkori-herding.title: Earliest Herders of the Central Sahara (Tadrart Acacus Mountains, Libya): A Punctuated Model for the Emergence of Pastoralism in Africa
di-lernia-2021-takarkori-herding.version: Journal of World Prehistory 34, 531–594, DOI 10.1007/s10963-021-09162-8. Issue year 2021, published online 4 January 2022.
di-lernia-2021-takarkori-herding.lineage: Primary report on direct bones and regional synthesis. Publication preview allowed access to the abstract and figure captions.

passages.locator: Abstract and caption of early cattle and caprine distribution maps, panel b

dunne-2012-takarkori-milk-lipids.title: First dairying in green Saharan Africa in the fifth millennium BC

grillo-2020-turkana-dairy-lipids.title: Molecular and isotopic evidence for milk, meat, and plants in prehistoric eastern African herder food systems
grillo-2020-turkana-dairy-lipids.version: Bristol repository accepted manuscript of PNAS 117, 9793–9799, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1920309117. Author list abbreviated.
grillo-2020-turkana-dairy-lipids.lineage: Primary lipid analyses. Site ages and broad subsistence descriptions also draw on previously published archaeology.

passages.locator: Table 1; Lipid residue results, Meat and milk
passages.note: Dongodien is assigned c. 5000–4500 cal BP. One of five interpretable Dongodien residues falls in the ruminant dairy range.

helmer-2005-euphrates-cattle-dimorphism.title: Identifying early domestic cattle from the Pre-Pottery Neolithic sites on the Middle Euphrates using sexual dimorphism
helmer-2005-euphrates-cattle-dimorphism.version: New Methods and the First Steps of Mammal Domestication, Oxbow Books, pp. 86–94. Author-posted version of the chapter.

passages.note: Dja’de male bones show greater size reduction from earlier comparisons than females. The authors assign Dja’de samples to 8800–8300 cal BCE and infer incipient domestication.

marsh-2026-palaeolithic-dogs.title: Dogs were widely distributed across western Eurasia during the Palaeolithic
marsh-2026-palaeolithic-dogs.version: Nature 651, 995–1003, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10170-x. UCL version-of-record PDF; author list abbreviated.
marsh-2026-palaeolithic-dogs.lineage: Primary direct specimen dates and nuclear genomes from Pınarbaşı and Gough’s Cave, distinct from the Bonn-Oberkassel material.

passages.locator: pp. 996–997, Dogs were widespread during the Palaeolithic; Fig. 1
passages.note: Identifies directly dated canids from Pınarbaşı and Gough’s Cave as dogs using nuclear DNA. The paper provides specimen-specific calibrated ranges.

meadow-1991-mehrgarh-cattle-bones.title: Faunal remains and urbanism at Harappa
meadow-1991-mehrgarh-cattle-bones.lineage: Chapter compares original faunal measurements from Mehrgarh, Nausharo and Harappa. The quoted chronological framework predates the new Mehrgarh enamel dates.

passages.locator: pp. 90–94, Figs. 7.1–7.2 and text on Bos
passages.note: The morphometric comparison distinguishes the occupational sequence and documents cattle size variation.

osypinska-2019-ludwinowo-fauna.title: Animal exploitation and meat consumption model: Archaeozoological analysis of osteological materials from the LBK settlement
osypinska-2019-ludwinowo-fauna.version: Ludwinowo, site 7: Neolithic settlement in Kuyavia, chapter 7.1, DOI 10.33547/ODA-SAH.08.Lud.07.1.
osypinska-2019-ludwinowo-fauna.lineage: Original zooarchaeological report on bones and teeth, distinct specimens and authors from the sherd lipid study.

passages.note: Cattle predominate in the Early Neolithic faunal assemblage. The authors infer livestock exploitation for meat and secondary products; small ruminants may have supplied milk too.

roffet-salque-2019-ludwinowo-vessels.title: Chronological and spatial trends in pottery use revealed through lipid residue analyses of LBK pottery vessels
roffet-salque-2019-ludwinowo-vessels.version: Ludwinowo, site 7: Neolithic settlement in Kuyavia, chapter 9, DOI 10.33547/ODA-SAH.08.Lud.09.
roffet-salque-2019-ludwinowo-vessels.lineage: Site-specific organic-residue analysis. Reuses Salque et al. 2013 measurements for sieves and adds new analyses mostly from other vessel forms; distinct evidence stream from the bones.

passages.note: Places dairy-bearing perforated vessels at Ludwinowo in LBK phases IIB and III.

smyth-2023-ludwinowo-husbandry.title: Integrated approaches to understanding animal exploitation and dairying in the Central European Early Neolithic: a case study from Ludwinowo 7 (Kuyavia, Poland; c. 5250–5000 cal BC)
smyth-2023-ludwinowo-husbandry.version: Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, DOI 10.3389/fearc.2023.1187087. Author list abbreviated.
smyth-2023-ludwinowo-husbandry.lineage: Integrated analysis combines cattle mortality profiles and tooth isotopes with ceramics. The tooth isotopes build on Kendall et al. 2019, and the sherd results include Salque et al. 2013 and the expanded 2019 assemblage.

passages.note: Cattle age and isotopic profiles support mixed meat and milk husbandry with seasonal calving. The integrated evidence identifies cows as the probable main milk source.

stiner-2022-asikli-herding-sequence.title: An endemic pathway to sheep and goat domestication at Aşıklı Höyük (Central Anatolia, Turkey)
stiner-2022-asikli-herding-sequence.version: PNAS 119, e2110930119, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2110930119. Author list abbreviated.
stiner-2022-asikli-herding-sequence.lineage: Expanded faunal study of the Aşıklı sequence with excavator overlap with the 2014 study. Includes Level 5 and reassesses caprine management through time.

passages.locator: Abstract; Results; Discussion, The Domesticatory Process at Aşıklı Höyük
passages.note: The authors infer initial small-scale management around 8400 cal BCE, followed by more substantial captive reproduction and livestock production.

colledge-2018-dhra-plant-remains.title: Plant domestication, production intensification and food storage at Pre-Pottery Neolithic A Dhra‘
colledge-2018-dhra-plant-remains.version: Levant, online version dated 17 January 2018, doi:10.1080/00758914.2018.1424746
colledge-2018-dhra-plant-remains.lineage: Author-uploaded full text of the online version, with the two authors shown in that copy. Analyzes charred macroremains from the same excavation as Kuijt and Finlayson’s architecture and preliminary phytolith study.

passages.locator: Dhra′ cereal densities, context 2134 and table 5
passages.note: A flotation sample from the layer between the floor and collapsed material in Structure 4 yielded charred barley grains at an above-average density for the site. The evidence concerns this sampled deposit associated with Structure 4.

douche-willcox-2018-aswad-barley.title: New archaeobotanical data from the Early Neolithic sites of Dja’de el-Mughara and Tell Aswad (Syria)
douche-willcox-2018-aswad-barley.lineage: Author-hosted copy of the version of record. The study uses a subset of secure contexts and revises an earlier published analysis that also involved Willcox.

passages.note: Using secure Pre-Pottery Neolithic B contexts and a revised stratigraphy, the authors report that domestic-type barley spikelet bases first form a substantial share in phase AW2. Table 1 dates AW2 to approximately 8200–7500 cal BCE.

groman-yaroslavski-2016-ohalo-harvesting.title: Composite Sickles and Cereal Harvesting Methods at 23,000-Years-Old Ohalo II, Israel
groman-yaroslavski-2016-ohalo-harvesting.lineage: Publisher version. The five blades constitute different specimens from the Ohalo II grains and grinding slab analyzed in earlier studies by overlapping teams.

passages.note: Cutting wear on five flint blades resembles experimental wear from cutting near-ripe cereal stems. Two blades, AL73c and AJ39c, carry wear interpreted as evidence of hafting.
Most recovered grains were fully ripe. The excavated grain assemblage need not be the harvest represented by these tools.

pedersen-2026-shubayqa-ground-stone.title: From Stone to Food: Foodways and Ground Stone Tools During the Natufian and Early Neolithic of Eastern Jordan
pedersen-2026-shubayqa-ground-stone.lineage: Publisher full text hosted on ResearchGate. Its artefact analysis uses different archaeological objects from the 2018 bread-fragment study with partly overlapping authors.

passages.locator: Section 3.1, Shubayqa Sites, Setting and Dating
passages.note: The Early Natufian phases 4–7 span approximately 14,800–14,100 cal BP at 68.2% using IntCal20.

passages.locator: Section 4.1, Early Natufian Use-Wear, table 2 and fig. 4
passages.note: In Early Natufian Shubayqa 1, wear on a handstone suggests seed or cereal grinding. Wear on a combined quern and mortar and nearby tool is consistent with grinding or pounding tubers or similar soft plants. The excavators compare these traces with food remains of the same broad period.

passages.locator: End of section 3, immediately before GST Use-Wear Results
passages.note: The authors flag the small early sample and ambiguity of use-wear interpretations.

weide-2018-chogha-golan-wild-grasses.title: A systematic review of wild grass exploitation in relation to emerging cereal cultivation throughout the Epipalaeolithic and aceramic Neolithic of the Fertile Crescent
weide-2018-chogha-golan-wild-grasses.lineage: PubMed Central full text. The study adds 23 earlier flotation samples from horizons VII to III and reuses previously analyzed horizon II samples from the same site.

passages.locator: Chogha Golan, Sampling and laboratory methods, and Conclusion
passages.note: Study of the local sequence records a decline in the relative representation of wild grasses when domesticated emmer becomes prominent around 9,800 cal BP. The authors consider the evidence insufficient to determine whether the earlier wild cereals were cultivated.

allue-2026-gesher-firewood.title: Paleoenvironmental and behavioral insights into firewood selection by early Middle Pleistocene hominins
allue-2026-gesher-firewood.version: Quaternary Science Reviews 382, 109973. Publisher abstract and version of record transcribed on ResearchGate.
allue-2026-gesher-firewood.lineage: New charcoal analysis of excavated Level 1 specimens, compared against earlier published wood, flint and fish material from the same horizon. Two authors also worked on the fish study. Inspected transcription at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/405546157_Paleoenvironmental_and_behavioral_insights_into_firewood_selection_by_early_Middle_Pleistocene_hominins.

passages.note: The study identifies 188 of 266 charcoal specimens recovered from Layer II-6 Level 1 (MIS 18). Ash and olive predominate in both charcoal and the comparison wood assemblage.

The largest charcoal cluster overlaps the main concentration of fish teeth in Level 1. Charcoal and burnt flint distributions do not precisely coincide. The maps include 190 charcoal fragments with full spatial records, 754 burnt flint microartifacts and 2471 fish remains.
The authors infer that hominins gathered available wood for fuel, with lakeshore deadwood or driftwood the likely source. They leave the significance of particular taxa in the cluster open.

galili-1997-kfar-samir-oil-excavation.title: Evidence for Earliest Olive-Oil Production in Submerged Settlements off the Carmel Coast, Israel
galili-1997-kfar-samir-oil-excavation.version: Journal of Archaeological Science 24(12), 1141–1150. Published article transcription on ResearchGate.
galili-1997-kfar-samir-oil-excavation.lineage: Original 1990s excavation and interpretation of Kfar Samir installations. Inspected publication copy at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/248578882_Evidence_for_Earliest_OliveOil_Production_in_Submerged_Settlements_off_the_Carmel_Coast_Israel. The comparison in Galili et al. (2021) and the proposed basketwork use in Rosenberg et al. (2023) cite these excavations.

passages.note: In pit 6, crushed and whole olive stones and pulp were recovered in alternating layers with organic clay above pebbles. The fill also contained reed and straw fragments.

The authors explain the deposits as residues of oil extraction, suggest some reed or straw elements could have acted as strainers, and compare the basket photograph with later olive-processing containers. The analogy does not identify a particular basket as the tool used in pit 6.

langgut-2024-tel-tsaf-olive-dating.title: The core area of fruit-tree cultivation: central Jordan Valley (Levant), ca. 7000 BP
langgut-2024-tel-tsaf-olive-dating.version: Palynology 48(4), 2347905. Publisher record and version of record transcribed on Academia.edu.
langgut-2024-tel-tsaf-olive-dating.lineage: Same lead researcher and Tel Tsaf Area C context as the 2022 study. Table 2 adds a direct olive assay and reproduces the earlier fig date. Inspected copy at https://www.academia.edu/121002056/The_core_area_of_fruit_tree_cultivation_central_Jordan_Valley_Levant_ca_7000_BP_Langgut_2024_PALYNOLOGY.

passages.note: Tel Tsaf Area C olive branch Beta-657404 yields 7160–6950 cal BP at 68.2% probability. Fig twig Beta-585311 yields 6960–6860 cal BP at the same probability and is carried over from Langgut and Garfinkel (2022).

The author interprets the olive charcoal beyond the tree's natural range as cultivation. The Carmel coast and Galilee are proposed as possible earlier areas. The summarized evidence does not identify a source orchard, a route or the people who moved the planting material.

quibell-1900-hierakonpolis-scorpion-mace.title: Hierakonpolis. Part I. Plates of Discoveries in 1898
quibell-1900-hierakonpolis-scorpion-mace.version: Egyptian Research Account, Fourth Memoir, London, Bernard Quaritch, 1900, with notes on plates by Petrie. Petrie Project transcription and facsimile entry.
quibell-1900-hierakonpolis-scorpion-mace.lineage: Original excavation publication of the object, including a developed drawing. The interpretation in the plate notes is an early reading of the same carved witness cited by Manning.

passages.locator: pp. 9–10, note to Pl. XXVIc and Pl. XXVIc
passages.note: The note reads the scene as a king inaugurating irrigation works and identifies figures working at a canal. It does not claim the depiction records transverse basin dykes or a measured canal network.
passages.quote: Two men are engaged in making the banks on opposite sides of a canal

rosenberg-2023-carmel-wood-and-basketry.title: The Unseen Record: Ninth–Seventh Millennia Cal. BP Wooden and Basketry Objects from Submerged Settlements off the Carmel Coast, Israel
rosenberg-2023-carmel-wood-and-basketry.lineage: Original technical description of KS 2 and archaeological context. The possible oil-processing function refers back to Galili et al. (1997), a coauthored earlier excavation study.

passages.note: Three fragments of a twig basket, possibly from the base and walls, exhibit alternate pair-twining and were recovered alongside olive pits and wood fragments in a clay-filled pit at Kfar Samir. The authors propose a possible aqal-like oil-processing use.
passages.quote: The vessel was braided by the alternate pair-twining method.

passages.note: The authors date KS 2 by the site chronology, with outer bounds of 7964–6299 cal BP across the reported sample intervals. The basket itself was not directly dated.

terral-2021-hishuley-olive-shape.title: The Shape Diversity of Olive Stones Resulting from Domestication and Diversification Unveils Traits of the Oldest Known 6500-Years-Old Table Olives from Hishuley Carmel Site (Israel)
terral-2021-hishuley-olive-shape.lineage: Geometric morphometric comparisons using ancient stone samples from the same Hishuley Carmel structures and a broader modern reference collection. Galili, Terral, Barazani and Dag also coauthored the original 2021 preservation study.

passages.locator: Materials and Methods, section 2.1; Discussion and Conclusions, Fig. 7
passages.note: The outline analysis finds ancient stones resembling both presumed wild and modern cultivated forms. Some more complex morphotypes are interpreted as signs of selection. This does not identify the source of the olives or the curing material.

willems-2017-nile-basin-debate.title: The Analysis of Historical Maps as an Avenue to the Interpretation of Pre-Industrial Irrigation Practices in Egypt
willems-2017-nile-basin-debate.version: The Nile: Natural and Cultural Landscape in Egypt, pp. 255–344. Publisher PDF at https://www.inlibra.com/document/download/pdf/uuid/486029aa-9cbf-38b8-83f4-dffa90a07aa9?page=1&toc=5723285.
willems-2017-nile-basin-debate.lineage: Historical-map and archaeological analysis. Early hydraulic interpretations on the cited pages discuss Butzer and Schenkel. The separate Fifth Dynasty relief is cited to Willems (2012), pp. 1101–1107.

passages.note: Schenkel disputed that the Scorpion macehead depicts an irrigation canal. The authors cite a scene in Niuserre's separate Fifth Dynasty sun temple as showing a dyke around a flooded basin and distinguish early local basins from later extensive networks.

arpin-2017-xianrendong-formation-and-pot.title: Site formation processes and site use in the Late Pleistocene and Early Holocene: micromorphology and FTIR analysis at the cave sites of Xianrendong and Yuchanyan
arpin-2017-xianrendong-formation-and-pot.lineage: Dissertation includes detailed original geoarchaeological observations. Arpin coauthored Wu et al. 2012. The techniques describe the same excavation research and earlier ceramic assemblage reports.

passages.note: The earliest West Area sherds in layers 3C1B and 3C1A were described as slab-joined and sometimes stripe-marked. Later 3B2 and above has examples with coiling and paddle impressions. Same site sequence does not establish continuous occupation or origin of the later technique.

baldi-2014-ceramic-workshops-tell-feres.title: Ceramic production and management of the fire between late Ubaid and LC1. The potter’s kilns of Tell Feres al-Sharqi
baldi-2014-ceramic-workshops-tell-feres.version: Proceedings of the 8th International Congress on the Archaeology of the Ancient Near East, vol. 3, pp. 187–200.
baldi-2014-ceramic-workshops-tell-feres.lineage: Original workshop account by a co-investigator in the later wheel study, with the same excavation underlying both accounts.

passages.note: Reports a multi-phase late Ubaid pottery workshop with kilns and potters’ implements, including two ceramic disc fragments interpreted as possible turntables.

baldi-roux-2016-wheel-coiling-comparison.title: The innovation of the potter’s wheel: a comparative perspective between Mesopotamia and the southern Levant
baldi-roux-2016-wheel-coiling-comparison.lineage: Publisher-formatted original case study of excavated ceramics. Shares Baldi and part of the Tell Feres assemblage with the 2021 study.

passages.locator: The potter’s wheel in northern Mesopotamia: a view from Tell Feres al-Sharqi; Fig. 2
passages.note: A late Ubaid workshop, about 4700 BCE, had a small clay disc with a slight socket, compatible with a pivot. Evidence of rotational energy used during wheel-coiling begins later in levels 5–4B and 4A, about 3900–3800 BCE.
Early southern Levant wheel-coiling predates the northern Mesopotamian finds. Neither independent innovation nor diffusion from the southern Levant is demonstrated.

file.representation: PDF of original publication or repository copy

craig-2021-prehistoric-fermentation-mark.title: Prehistoric Fermentation, Delayed-Return Economies, and the Adoption of Pottery Technology
craig-2021-prehistoric-fermentation-mark.lineage: Independent methodological assessment in the publisher’s article. It does not re-assay the Godin or Georgian sherds.

passages.locator: Direct Evidence for Prehistoric Fermented Beverages
passages.note: For Godin Tepe, cautions that the Feigl spot test lacks specificity and that oxalates can be present in other materials. For wine residues, chemical markers such as tartaric acid need contextual support.

drieu-2020-context-and-specificity-wine-.title: Is it possible to identify ancient wine production using biomolecular approaches?
drieu-2020-context-and-specificity-wine-.version: STAR: Science & Technology of Archaeological Research 6(1), pp. 16–29.
drieu-2020-context-and-specificity-wine-.lineage: Independent methodological assessment and original analyses of separate Zamostje 2 samples.

passages.note: Tartaric acid can occur in vessels beyond the plausible range of ancient wine contact. For grape juice or wine interpretation the archaeological context and comparative chemistry matter.

gopnik-2016-godin-ceramic-provenance.title: A view from the east: The Godin VI Oval and the Uruk Sphere
gopnik-2016-godin-ceramic-provenance.version: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 7, pp. 835–848, doi:10.1016/j.jasrep.2016.02.020.
gopnik-2016-godin-ceramic-provenance.lineage: Full publisher-formatted article displayed by author on Academia. Independent ceramic provenance measurements, not replication of the residue test.

passages.note: A sherd of the paired-handled type, GOT_20, has Godin Main fabric associated with a local clay source. Fig. 5 compares the type with Hamoukar. The study does not identify GOT_20 as the sherd that yielded the 1993 oxalate test.
The assemblages inside and outside the Oval were more integrated than an earlier enclave interpretation suggested. Vessel style alone was not a reliable proxy for clay provenance.

huysecom-2009-ounjougou-first-pottery.title: The emergence of pottery in Africa during the tenth millennium cal BC: new evidence from Ounjougou (Mali)
huysecom-2009-ounjougou-first-pottery.lineage: University of Geneva scan of the original field study. The 2020 synthesis discusses the same HA1 finds.

passages.locator: pp. 909–911, HA1 formation and assemblage; Figs. 1 and 3
passages.note: The sherds were redeposited in fluvial unit HA1, under dated units. HA1 itself could not be directly dated. The assemblage includes a bowl fragment and a decorated body fragment.

A few earlier or contemporary African comparisons have possible but problematic associations. Grass exploitation is an environmental and technological interpretation, not an identification of vessel contents.

file.representation: PDF of original publication or repository copy

liu-2024-shangshan-rice-beer-microfossil.title: Identification of 10,000-year-old rice beer at Shangshan in the Lower Yangzi River valley of China
liu-2024-shangshan-rice-beer-microfossil.lineage: Original study with a partially overlapping research group and a distinct site and specimen assemblage.

passages.note: Globular jars from the early Shangshan phase, circa 10,000–9,000 cal BP, yield rice and fungal microfossils interpreted as rice beer made with a mould starter.

liu-2026-jiahu-brewing-microfossils.title: Revisiting Jiahu’s 9000-Year-Old Fermented Beverage: New Microfossil Evidence for Early Qu-Based and Malt-Based Brewing Technologies in North China
liu-2026-jiahu-brewing-microfossils.lineage: Publisher’s original open-access PDF. Supplement PDF extracted from publisher ZIP https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/heritage/heritage-09-00335/article_deploy/heritage-09-00335-s001.zip (ZIP SHA-256 aa664f5aed29cdcde7f534b549704d297a02efef8e2d9c9e2c5e2fca8ea938a0). Juzhong Zhang also coauthored the 2004 study. Different assays, a shared find context and unverified overlap of individual sherds.

passages.note: Liu and colleagues describe damaged starch, rice and abundant Monascus-like remains in jar and bottle interiors. They infer qu-like saccharification and some possible malt processing. The molecular evidence for honey and fruit is weaker, though these ingredients remain possible.

The newer sampling context identifiers include POT8 from ash pit T14H32. The 2004 paper’s note 10 lists T14/H32, confirming common context nomenclature without uniquely identifying the same physical fragment.

file.representation: PDF of original publication or repository copy

michel-mcgovern-badler-1993-godin-beer.title: The First Wine & Beer: Chemical Detection of Ancient Fermented Beverages
michel-mcgovern-badler-1993-godin-beer.lineage: Authors’ project site displays scan of publisher article. Read through the web index. Direct download failed. The same authors published the initial 1992 Nature letter.

passages.note: The authors give approximately 3500–2900 BCE for their Period V context.

Yellow deposits in interior crisscross grooves of a double-handled jug tested positive in the Feigl spot test for oxalate. Exterior scrapings and a wine jar sample were negative. The authors infer beer from the assay and vessel analogies, and propose barley because six-row barley dominated sampled botanical remains from Period V.

nieuwenhuyse-2010-earliest-tell-sabi-aby.title: Not so coarse, nor always plain: the earliest pottery of Syria
nieuwenhuyse-2010-earliest-tell-sabi-aby.lineage: Original excavated assemblage and chronology, in the university repository. Later histories reuse these excavation results.

passages.locator: Abstract; early phases and ceramics discussion
passages.note: The earliest stratified Sabi Abyad vessels around 7000 BCE are small, mineral-tempered and sometimes decorated. The findspot of the earliest wares does not establish where they were originally made.

file.representation: PDF of original publication or repository copy

nieuwenhuyse-2015-tell-sabi-abyad-potter.title: Tracing pottery use and the emergence of secondary product exploitation through lipid residue analysis at Late Neolithic Tell Sabi Abyad (Syria)
nieuwenhuyse-2015-tell-sabi-abyad-potter.version: Journal of Archaeological Science 64, pp. 54–66, doi:10.1016/j.jas.2015.10.002.
nieuwenhuyse-2015-tell-sabi-abyad-potter.lineage: Original vessel lipid assays, distinct from the stratigraphic study of earliest pottery and from faunal observations. Evershed et al. 2008 and the 2018 chapter partly report this same sample series.

passages.note: Sample SAB263 from Operation IV, Grey Burnished Ware, has a ruminant dairy signature in a ca. 6400–6330 cal BCE context. Samples SAB2 and SAB173 from Dark-Faced Burnished Ware and SAB214 from Standard Fine Ware are assigned ruminant dairy in contexts dated ca. 6000–5900 cal BCE.

The specific animal species and milk products cannot be inferred. The study compares the sherd evidence with independently observed faunal age profiles. The authors report later mixed meat and secondary-product exploitation as a plausible interpretation.

file.representation: PDF of original publication or repository copy

van-der-plicht-2012-tell-sabi-abyad-faun.title: Tell Sabi Abyad, Syria: An Interpretation of Stable Isotope Values of Faunal Bone Collagen
van-der-plicht-2012-tell-sabi-abyad-faun.version: Radiocarbon 54(3–4), pp. 281–289, doi:10.1017/S003382220004707X. Cambridge’s web release is dated 2016.
van-der-plicht-2012-tell-sabi-abyad-faun.lineage: Original faunal specimens and measurements, with overlapping site investigators. A separate observational line about herd management, not a duplicate sherd assay.

passages.note: Faunal assemblages and stable isotope measurements document local herds and management changes. The cited milk attribution itself comes from ceramic residue and zooarchaeological studies; the bone isotopes alone do not identify a dairy product.

huang-2003-caoxieshan-paddy-pollen-phyto.title: Pollen and phytolith records from primitive paddy fields during the Neolithic at Caoxieshan, Taihu Plain, southern China
huang-2003-caoxieshan-paddy-pollen-phyto.version: Terra Australis 19, chapter 14, in Phytolith and starch research in the Australian-Pacific-Asian regions; ANU repository scan.
huang-2003-caoxieshan-paddy-pollen-phyto.lineage: Original analyses of pollen and phytolith samples from field pits and archaeological layers, paired with the Caoxieshan excavation evidence.

passages.note: Pit S13 is interpreted as a natural depression by a natural ditch. Pits S′ and S15 have artificial features including ditches and furrows.

passages.locator: pp. 167–169, Table 2 and Fig. 3; p. 172 conclusions
passages.note: The authors report rice pollen and phytoliths and a decline in pondweed-family pollen between their phases. They interpret the decline as falling local water levels and propose that changes in available water prompted construction of the artificial system. The chapter’s Majiabang terminology and phase dating are left as reported.

kudo-2010-shimoyakebe-plant-remains.title: Characterization of Plant Remains on Jomon Potteries Excavated from the Shimo-yakebe Site, Tokyo, Japan
kudo-2010-shimoyakebe-plant-remains.version: Bulletin of the National Museum of Japanese History 158, 1–26, author report in Japanese with English summary.
kudo-2010-shimoyakebe-plant-remains.lineage: Original dating and context report, also used in the later comparative seed study coauthored by Sasaki. This overlaps the specimen in Lee and colleagues.

passages.locator: Table 1, SY 37, PLD-9088; Results and English summary
passages.note: A charred Glycine sp. seed from walnut midden no. 1 is reported as 4335 ± 30 radiocarbon years BP. This is the same lab code cited by Lee and colleagues. The report places the seed in the Middle Jomon; the number 4335 is a radiocarbon determination.

nakajima-2019-common-carp-aquaculture.title: Common carp aquaculture in Neolithic China dates back 8,000 years
nakajima-2019-common-carp-aquaculture.version: Nature Ecology & Evolution 3, pp. 1415–1418 (2019); full publisher text inspected through a mirror.

passages.quote: was present at the Early Neolithic Jiahu site, Henan Province, China, by around 6000 bc

passages.note: Dates the three Jiahu phases; Period III has two modal groups of estimated body lengths. The assemblage has a relatively high proportion of common carp.

Infers a stage of management in marshy waters. The measured remains are not a direct witness of any particular pond or channel; the model draws on comparison with archaeological and recent Japanese specimens.

file.method: Passages of about 500 characters either side of each cited quotation, cut from the fetched page text.

nakajima-2019-common-carp-aquaculture.lineage: Article of record at the DOI. Its text, figures and methods were read at https://www.academia.edu/167862178/Common_carp_aquaculture_in_Neolithic_China_dates_back_8_000_years. The retained repository excerpt covers the abstract.

shu-2012-kuahuqiao-burning-interpretatio.title: Did alder (Alnus) fires trigger rice cultivation in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River, East China?
shu-2012-kuahuqiao-burning-interpretatio.lineage: Separate pollen, phytolith and microscopic-charcoal study of the same locality. Only the abstract was inspected.

passages.note: The authors dispute Zong and colleagues’ identification of the burned vegetation as predominantly alder, interpreting their material as evidence of oak and pine woodland burning before rice cultivation.

sterckx-2025-fish-farming-texts.title: Fish Farming in Pre-modern China: A Study and Translation of Two Texts
sterckx-2025-fish-farming-texts.lineage: Original textual analysis and translation of surviving witnesses to historical fish farming; contextual comparison to Nakajima et al. cites their own dataset.

passages.note: Traces the fish farming text attributed to Fan Li, whose earliest transmitted version survives in the sixth-century CE Qimin yaoshu. The attribution and the title in a later catalogue do not date the work to the historical Fan Li.

wang-2022-shangshan-stone-flake-rice-har.title: New evidence for rice harvesting in the early Neolithic Lower Yangtze River, China
wang-2022-shangshan-stone-flake-rice-har.version: PLOS ONE, 17(12), e0278200; version of record.
wang-2022-shangshan-stone-flake-rice-har.lineage: Original use-wear and phytolith residue analyses on excavated flakes, distinct from the Shangshan sediment phytolith samples used to infer domestication traits.

passages.locator: Integrating use-wear and phytolith results, Figs. 6–8
passages.note: Specimen SS-10 from Shangshan combines predominantly transverse striations with rice-husk phytoliths, interpreted as cutting panicles. Botanical residues and use-wear provide different proxies on the same flakes.

The authors propose that repeated selective panicle harvest can bias seed stocks towards non-shattering rice if later harvests are kept for sowing. SS-10 directly informs the technique but does not test seed selection for a particular population or the silica traits studied by Zuo and colleagues.

zhao-2020-donghulin-flotation.title: 北京东胡林遗址植物遗存浮选结果及分析 (Plant remains unearthed at the Donghulin site in Beijing: discussion on results of flotation)
zhao-2020-donghulin-flotation.version: Kaogu (Archaeology) 2020 no. 7, pp. 99–106, Chinese original presented with the ResearchGate item for the 2021 English translation (DOI 10.1515/char-2021-0015).
zhao-2020-donghulin-flotation.lineage: Original report on charred remains from flotation. Several authors overlap with the Yang et al. starch study, but the specimens and analyses are distinct.

passages.note: Report of 14 charred specimens assigned morphologically to foxtail millet (Setaria italica), one assigned to broomcorn millet and 11 to green foxtail (Setaria viridis).

passages.locator: pp. 103–104, chronology and caution about displacement
passages.note: Four deposit units yielded the foxtail millet grains. Four pooled grains from one unit were too small for the attempted direct AMS date. A cork-tree seed from a deposit also containing charred foxtail millet was directly dated as BA07888, 8885 ± 55 radiocarbon years BP, calibrated to 8240–7820 BCE at 95.4%. This is a context date for one millet-bearing unit.

zheng-2007-kuahuqiao-rice-rachillae.title: Characteristics of the short rachillae of rice from archaeological sites dating to 7000 years ago
zheng-2007-kuahuqiao-rice-rachillae.version: Chinese Science Bulletin 52, 1654–1660 (2007), DOI 10.1007/s11434-007-0258-1; publisher PDF.
zheng-2007-kuahuqiao-rice-rachillae.lineage: Original morphological analysis of rice grains and husks from excavated material, distinct from the sediment microfossils examined by Zong and colleagues.

passages.note: The authors assign 70 of the 120 short rachillae they examined from Kuahuqiao to wild type and 50 to a japonica type, and infer early rice cultivation. Morphological categories and samples do not identify individual fields or exact generations of plants.

The team separately reports examples of wild-type and japonica-type rachilla markings in Shangshan and Xiaohuangshan material. Their rice material and morphology differ from the dated Shangshan silica samples analysed by Zuo and colleagues.

zong-2007-kuahuqiao-wetland-cultivation.title: Fire and flood management of coastal swamp enabled first rice paddy cultivation in east China
zong-2007-kuahuqiao-wetland-cultivation.lineage: Original palaeoecological study of an excavation-face sediment sequence and associated archaeological contexts.

passages.note: The authors place their studied cultural sediments in a modelled interval of about 7700–7550 cal BP. This interpretation concerns one excavated sequence.

Pollen, algal and fungal indicators, diatoms and microscopic charcoal are used to infer sustained wetland rice cultivation. Clearance and later maintenance are interpretations of changes in vegetation and fire indicators. Low-level brackish inflow is observed indirectly; a protective barrier is hypothesised.

goren-2025-complex-metallurgy-nahal-mish.title: The Advent of Complex Metallurgy
goren-2025-complex-metallurgy-nahal-mish.version: IMEKO TC26 International Conference on Metrology for Archaeology and Cultural Heritage, pp. 339–344
goren-2025-complex-metallurgy-nahal-mish.lineage: Full proceedings version. Reports measurements on Southern Levantine finds independent of the Mehrgarh study.

passages.note: Organic inclusions from selected ceramic cores of cast objects were dated. The authors report a production interval of about 4700–3800 BCE and explicitly caution that the age of the Mehrgarh object is based on deposition context, so strict priority remains uncertain.

odler-2021-arsenical-copper-tools-giza.title: Arsenical copper tools of Old Kingdom Giza craftsmen: First data
odler-2021-arsenical-copper-tools-giza.version: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 36, article 102868
odler-2021-arsenical-copper-tools-giza.lineage: Version of record inspected in the author-posted facsimile at https://www.academia.edu/45502657/Arsenical_copper_tools_of_Old_Kingdom_Giza_craftsmen_First_data. The material is from an independent archaeological context relative to the earlier mortuary assemblage.

passages.note: Fifteen finished artefacts were analysed from the Kromer settlement debris dump at Giza. Sealings associate the material with the Khufu and Khafra reigns (c. 2500–2450 BCE in the authors' chronology). The deposit combined discarded material, and the finds cannot be assigned separately to either reign.
The examined functional full-size chisel and two probable axe-blade fragments were arsenical copper. The authors infer carpentry among the activities represented in the debris.

radivojevic-2021-belovode-metal-producti.title: Belovode: technology of metal production
radivojevic-2021-belovode-metal-producti.version: The Rise of Metallurgy in Eurasia, Archaeopress, chapter 11, pp. 123–151
radivojevic-2021-belovode-metal-producti.lineage: Open UCL deposit of the published chapter. Same analytical project lineage as earlier Belovode reports, but the excavated Trench 18 finds and their dating associations are from a separate 2012–2013 campaign.

passages.note: Slag, a slagged sherd and a metal droplet are reported from Trench 18 spit 5 in spatial association with Feature 6; the reported Feature 6 contextual sample MAMS23380 is 4724–4555 cal BCE, 2σ. Approximate assemblage placement is the 47th century BCE.

passages.locator: pp. 128–129 and 133–138, installation discussion and analysis
passages.note: The authors infer that Feature 6 may have been a pottery-lined pit for smelting from the burnt pit and the nearby slagged sherds. Feature 35 is a separate possibility with a different evidentiary basis.
New slag and related finds are consistent with the use of manganese-rich black-and-green ore reported in earlier excavations.

radivojevic-2021-plocnik-metal-productio.title: Pločnik: technology of metal production
radivojevic-2021-plocnik-metal-productio.version: The Rise of Metallurgy in Eurasia, Archaeopress, chapter 26, pp. 301–316
radivojevic-2021-plocnik-metal-productio.lineage: Repository metadata and full facsimile at https://www.academia.edu/69498047/Ch26_Radivojevi%C4%87_Rehren_Plo%C4%8Dnik_technology_of_metal_production_from_Radivojevi%C4%87_Roberts_et_al_2021_The_Rise_of_Metallurgy_in_Eurasia. Original finds from the 2012–2013 excavations.

passages.note: Copper ring C_P2/13 was found at Trench 24, spit 9, Horizon 1, associated with Feature 3. The associated sample MAMS22081 dates to 4493–4365 cal BCE (2σ).

Figure 12 documents annealing twins and slip lines in C_P2/13. The ring is one of several high-purity copper artefacts. P10/13 is a distinct copper foil, separate from the earlier tin-bronze foil reported in 2013. The broader new assemblage supports secondary processing at Pločnik.

radivojevic-2021-vinca-copper-supply-net.title: Metallurgical knowledge and networks of supply in the 5th millennium BC Balkans: Belovode and Pločnik in their regional context
radivojevic-2021-vinca-copper-supply-net.version: The Rise of Metallurgy in Eurasia, Archaeopress, chapter 41, pp. 484–527
radivojevic-2021-vinca-copper-supply-net.lineage: Open UCL deposit of the published chapter. Joint study of distinct archaeological samples, combined with older published comparative data. Shared authorship and specimens with chapters 11 and 26 do not provide independent replication of the transfer inference.

passages.note: The Pločnik ordinary-copper band or ring C_P2/13 and Belovode Feature 6 metal droplet B47/12/3 and slagged sherd B23/12 form a dispersed group in lead-isotope ratios. The cluster is consistent with related geological feedstocks.

passages.locator: Group 3 source comparison, Fig. 7 and Table 6
passages.note: A distinct Pločnik copper chisel HDM1586 matches the Belovode droplet B47/12/3. The authors propose a supply route from Belovode for the chisel, and the wider Group 3 isotope field does not match any identified Balkan ore deposit.
P10/13 and Belovode copper droplet Bf21/12 have similar trace-element profiles and belong to a group that also includes production evidence from Gornja Tuzla.

sanger-2018-early-copper-mcqueen-shell-r.title: Early metal use and crematory practices in the American Southeast
sanger-2018-early-copper-mcqueen-shell-r.lineage: Full published paper in PubMed Central. The analysed Georgia artefacts are distinct from Old Copper dating and lake sediment samples.

passages.locator: Results, Elemental Study of Copper Objects, Fig. 4 and Table 2
passages.note: Copper from the McQueen Shell Ring most closely matches tested deposits around northern Lake Superior, with Minong on Isle Royale the highest probability among tested options. The two sets of measurements examine the same archaeological assemblage.
The directly dated bone samples from the upper burial give 4100–3980 cal BP. This dates the associated deposit and leaves the metal's original extraction and working dates open.

dillehay-2012-huaca-prieta-chronology.title: Chronology, mound-building and environment at Huaca Prieta, coastal Peru, from 13 700 to 4000 years ago
dillehay-2012-huaca-prieta-chronology.version: Antiquity 86(331), pp. 48–70, DOI 10.1017/S0003598X00062451. Version-of-record copy hosted by coauthor Tiffiny Tung.
dillehay-2012-huaca-prieta-chronology.lineage: Original excavation chronology. Splitstoser and Dillehay also published the separate laboratory indigo analysis, which uses this chronology but samples a different textile from the independently dated yarn.

passages.locator: p. 56, Table 1, HP-3, AA82121 and AA86948

jolie-2011-guitarrero-fibre.title: Cordage, Textiles, and the Late Pleistocene Peopling of the Andes
jolie-2011-guitarrero-fibre.version: Current Anthropology 52(2), pp. 285–296, DOI 10.1086/659336. Rendered article copy cross-checked against journal and University of Nebraska metadata.
jolie-2011-guitarrero-fibre.lineage: Original direct dating and structural observations of material from the previously excavated cave. PDF from the institutional repository failed to download.

passages.note: OxA-21269 is two-ply cord, dated 12,130–11,800 cal BP. AA81781 and AA81782 are close and open twining, dated respectively 11,330–11,100 and 11,280–11,080 cal BP. The spiral-interlinked fragment AA81780 instead dates to 2310–2040 cal BP.

The close-twined piece is made from leaf fibre consistent with Agavaceae or Bromeliaceae. The open piece combines twisted yarns with whole rushlike stems. Coils and plant material support on-site fibre work. Proposed uses of the surviving fragments remain interpretive.

kistler-2018-maize-dispersal.title: Multiproxy evidence highlights a complex evolutionary legacy of maize in South America
kistler-2018-maize-dispersal.version: Science 362(6420), pp. 1309–1313, DOI 10.1126/science.aav0207. White Rose institutional repository accepted manuscript.
kistler-2018-maize-dispersal.lineage: Independent paleogenetic and modern landrace samples for regional crop ancestry, combined with a synthesis that cites the existing early archaeological dates. It does not date Par_N1 or identify an individual source settlement.

passages.note: Genomes support movement of an ancestral maize population from Mexico to South America, with domestication traits potentially still evolving after the move.

lanaud-2024-archaeogenomic-cacao.title: A revisited history of cacao domestication in pre-Columbian times revealed by archaeogenomic approaches
lanaud-2024-archaeogenomic-cacao.version: Scientific Reports 14, 2972, DOI 10.1038/s41598-024-53010-6. Version-of-record article rendered online.
lanaud-2024-archaeogenomic-cacao.lineage: Archaeogenomics and residues from other vessel assemblages. Several investigators overlap with the Santa Ana-La Florida project.

passages.note: Positive cacao DNA calls include Valdivia and San Jacinto cultural contexts. Table 1 gives broad ranges for the associated cultures. The authors distinguish multiple genetic affinities on the Ecuadorian and Colombian coast. The work does not trace descent from an individual Santa Ana-La Florida sample.

lavallee-1988-telarmachay.title: L’occupation préhistorique de l’abri de Telarmachay (Pérou) : un aspect de la néolithisation andine
lavallee-1988-telarmachay.version: Comptes rendus des séances de l’Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres 132(2), pp. 266–285, DOI 10.3406/crai.1988.14604. Persée scan.
lavallee-1988-telarmachay.lineage: Primary excavation synthesis reporting the original camelid mortality and dental interpretation from the Telarmachay project, including the analyses by Jane Wheeler.

passages.note: Older levels document a shift toward more specialized exploitation of camelids. A rise in fetal and neonatal remains and alpaca-like incisors in the subsequent sequence were interpreted as signs of domestication and confinement.

le-neun-2026-telarmachay-camelids.title: New insights into the domestication process of south American camelids at Telarmachay (Peru) from 9,000 to 4,500 years before present (BP)
le-neun-2026-telarmachay-camelids.version: Quaternary Science Reviews 376, 109819, DOI 10.1016/j.quascirev.2026.109819. Full article copy rendered online, publisher abstract checked.
le-neun-2026-telarmachay-camelids.lineage: Same rock shelter and legacy excavation corpus, shared Wheeler authorship. Adds separate shape, isotope, and mortality analyses, not a second excavation.

passages.note: Talus morphology changes in vicuña-like camelids in layer IV. The article interprets changed mobility as possible management intensification between modeled phase boundaries of 6.4–6.0 and 5.8–4.5 ka BP. The isotope results show no major change in diet or environment.
The reported bone morphology does not establish a shift to alpaca or llama phenotypes. The authors discuss protective herding as a possible alternative to captivity.

lombardo-2020-early-holocene-crop.title: Early Holocene crop cultivation and landscape modification in Amazonia
lombardo-2020-early-holocene-crop.version: Nature 581, pp. 190–193, DOI 10.1038/s41586-020-2162-7. Bern repository author manuscript, DOI 10.7892/boris.143456, rendered by CORE.

passages.note: Isla Manechi levels yielded a heart-shaped Manihot phytolith at approximately 10,350 cal BP and scalloped squash-rind phytoliths at approximately 10,250 cal BP. Squash measurements fall within a domesticated range. Site 575 had squash at approximately 9850 cal BP.

passages.locator: Evidence of early plant cultivation and Implication for biodiversity
passages.note: The authors give probable cultivation in fertile home gardens on the islands. They do not establish an in situ origin for the squash or a prepared planting surface in the earliest sampled strata.

roosevelt-1991-lower-amazon-pottery.title: Eighth Millennium Pottery from a Prehistoric Shell Midden in the Brazilian Amazon

The sherds are described as fragile, red-brown and grit-tempered. The authors discuss mobile humic acids and modern carbon as possible contaminants and report a broad error for the single TL assay. Riverine faunal remains contextualize the assemblage.

boethius-2016-norje-fish-pit.title: Something rotten in Scandinavia: The world's earliest evidence of fermentation
